reference_book.title: The Lightning Thief (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #1)
reference_book.review_text:
A demigod (both in the literal and figurative senses) goes to a lifeless summer camp before venturing off on a road trip tour across America with two camp buddies, running into the majority of Greek mythology along the way while he laughs in all of their faces and outsmarts everyone, only to be shocked when his sketchy, barely-developed, apparent best friend reveals himself to be a traitor. It's ok though, his betrayal and the threat of the world's ending can wait until after Percy and his friends return to summer camp next year - for now, they need to go back home for a year and ignore everything they've learned and discovered in the book. 
 Ok, maybe that two-sentence summary is a little unfair (this is a children's book after all), but The Lightning Thief has its fair share of problems as it falls into just about all of the usual tropes that plague children's/YA books. Its main fault is probably a lack of world-building. Riordan attempts to fuse the real world and Greek mythology is fine in theory, but a bit of a disaster in practice. The resulting world is poorly defined and rests on random splices of Greek mythology thrown in every few pages. There's really no sense of danger in the book as readers have no way of knowing the effects or ramifications of anything that happens in this fused world. 
 What bothered me most about this book was its failure as a developing narrative. Percy's encounters seem to be given purely to provide some action every chapter and really don't tie together very well from a character perspective. It feels like a bunch of scenarios spliced together rather than a story organically unfolding. Stuff happens, but it ends abruptly and then is quickly followed by some more stuff happening. While there is an overarching plot that ties these events together, the characters' progressions are token in nature, not meaningful. 
 All in all, young children will probably find a lot to like in this book. Manufactured excitement abounds. For older readers however, Percy Jackson is another lesson in synthetic storytelling which "checks all of the boxes," but fails to leave an impact.

book_a.title: The Sea of Monsters (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #2)

sample_reviews.review_text:
It's been a year since Percy Jackson learned that he is a demigod, the son of his human mother and Poseidon, the Greek God of the sea. On his last day of school, Percy hopes to finish the year without any major disasters and head off to Camp Half Blood, a summer camp for demigods. Unfortunately, trouble has a knack for finding Percy, and he has a run-in with some monsters in gym class. Saved by his friend Annabeth and his classmate Tyson, they escape to camp. 
 Camp Half Blood is not how Percy remembers it. The protective magical boundary of camp is collapsing, monsters are invading the borders, and the camp staff has changed. To make things worse, Percy keeps having dreams about his friend Grover, a satyr on a quest, being in danger. It turns out that Grover has created and "empathy link", allowing him to communicate with Percy from a distance. Between Grover, Hermes, and the Gray Sisters, Percy pieces together clues as to how he can save Camp Half Blood, as well as Grover. Percy's latest quest will take him to the Sea of Monsters, the fabled site of creatures such as Charybdis and the Sirens. In this sequel, Percy will take on old foes and new ones, make new friends, and discover more about his father and family. 
 One of the things I love most about this series is how covertly educational it is! Percy interacts with many characters from Greek mythology and Percy often recalls a quick line or two about the story behind those characters. I recall learning about mythology in grade school and it's fun to revisit those tales. Mention is also given to the works of Greek historians, and I must give kudos to Riordan for making Homer's Odyssey seem interesting! 
 I love how you never know what's going to happen next in this series. Yes, you know something isn't going to be as easy as it initially seems, but you never know who or what to expect! Riordan has a tendency of leading the reader to feel like the worst is over, and then suddenly he throws in another unexpected element. I enjoy guessing what is coming based on context clues (e.g. in book one, when they were at Auntie Em's Garden Emporium and there were tons of horrified looking stone statues- If you know your Greek mythology, you know Medusa is coming!). 
 The only thing that drove me nuts about this book was how oblivious Percy seems to have become. In the first book, he's not well versed in mythology so Annabeth and Grover are often explaining what things are to him. If I suddenly discovered that all of those stories I'd learned in school were in fact real, I'd head home and hit the books to learn as much as I possibly could. I'd also become more aware of my surroundings. Percy, however, seems to have gone home and left his demigod self at Camp Half Blood for the year. He is fully aware of the "mist" and how it keeps humans from perceiving otherworldly things, but allows himself to be fooled by it on multiple occasions. He also requires a great deal of explanation from Annabeth regarding mythological stories. Percy has obviously never heard the quote, "Know thy enemy"! 
 This book is by no means a difficult read. It's obviously geared towards a younger crowd, but adults can definitely enjoy it as well! I'm 23, and I love what I've read thus far! I even went ahead and bought the remainder of the series! This book took me a grand total of two days to read, but part of that was because I couldn't put it down. It's well written, and you have the opportunity to learn more about the key characters and their lives, as well as gain more of the history of Camp Half Blood. 
 This second installment in the Percy Jackson series is exciting and interesting, taking the reader to many new places along the East coast of the United States. If you've got a child, or even if you enjoy a light read yourself, this book is the second installment in a series that has many great elements- adventure, mythology, action and more! Check it out!
Bleh.
A cute, entertaining read, but nothing extraordinary.
Loved it!
2015 Reading Challenge: "a book with magic"

I absolutely LOVE this series and am so glad that I haven't seen any of the movies. Like I said after I read The Lightening Thief, at first I thought it was too similar to Harry Potter but I have changed my mind. There are, of course, similarities, but I think that's common in the genre. I got a lot out of this reading because I was teaching The Inferno and Oedipus to my students at the same time, so the Greek allusions had a big impact on me. I'm finding myself wishing there were more than 3 books in this series.
I AM SO READING THE THIRD!!
Lots of great plot twists. A fun read and a fun way to learn or brush up on Greek mythology and make it relate to current times.
Note to myself: Never dare to touch this series again

I am reading this for my nephew because he loves it. Unfortunately I don't share the same love but shhhh :) This is a little too 'young' for me... the author jumps around into one adventure after the other without really playing them out and they all seem super random to me. It's like... let's see how many crazy magical experiences we can jam pack into 1 book.

sample_reviews.review_text: I really enjoy how much these books teach readers about Greek mythology. It's very cool.
I didn't enjoy this book as much as the previous two, but I plan on continuing to read the series.
Loved it so much!! As always I love these characters! And gosh, this series is just amazing

This is the 3rd in the Percy Jackson series. It was a very fast read. Percy and Annabeth attempt to save two half-bloods, Bianca and Nico di Angelo. They are attacked by monsters (of course). They are saved by Artemis. Annabeth disappears and Artemis is kidnapped. Percy joins the Hunters and Campers who want to go on the quest to find them. The Oracle tells them that one of their group would die at their parent's hand. Will that be Percy,the son of Poseidon or Thalia the daughter of Zeus. The daughter of Athena,Atlas or Hades?
GENIUS
I don't really like Thalia and when she actually considered sacrificing Bessie, my estimation of her dropped below sea level.
This one did not hold my interest as much but I would give it four stars or higher in terms of me reading to my kids. I cannot wait to own this series and read to Fisher when he is a little older!
Another great installment in the Percy Jackson series. I have yet to be disappointed in these books. The more Percy grows the more I like him.
I didn't like it quite as much as the first or second but probably only because I wasn't crazy about some of the new characters.

Thumbs up for the appearances of Blackjack and Bessie. (This girl's heart is easily won be innocence, humour and animals. These are the combination!) 
 Another thumbs up for the heroic Zoe! I practically cried for her. Why? Read it and don't let first appearance fool you!

I feel like this book killed my brain cells. 
 I realise it may have been written for 4 year olds but still. 
 This book was just so... EMPTY. Alot of "somehow I knew", "suddenly it just happened" and "supriSinglys". Like tell the story properly.. 
 Learn things where I can see it. Don't just have super super intuition it boring. 
 And also.. All the chapter names were a summary of the chapter. Why... Why... Chapter 123 would have worked for me. 
 All the missions Percy went on reminded me very much of a video game.. Every step of the way there was some pathetic obstacle, he pressed "up, down, up, up, triangle, square, circle, up, r2" and it was over. So predictable and so meh.. 
 I'm reading the second one because im determined to get through.. I have hopes it will improve.

I've seen the movies and loved them so I thought it was about time I saw where everything began for Percy, Grover and Annabeth. The Lightning Thief by Rick Riordan tells the story of how twelve year old Percy Jackson discovers he's a demigod. Son of Poseidon, Percy has never quite been like other kids. Hidden in the mortal world to protect him from those with grudges against his biological father, Percy has always known that he was different. When Zeus' lightning bolt is stolen, Percy's existence comes to light and his paternity is revealed. If Percy is to find the bolt (and consequentially save his mother and become a hero) - he needs to overcome monsters and battle gods. Not alone in his quest, his best friend Grover and one of Athena's daughters, Annabeth, tag along to give Percy the best chance against the powerful immortals. 
 For the right audience, I believe this book would be perfect. There's action and adventure. A great take on classic mythology and characters I could fall in love with. 
 The problem is - I'm not the right audience. I'm in my twenties and unlike a lot of other young adult and middle grade books I've read - this one made me feel old in a way no other book I've read before has. 
 The characters, as entertaining as they are, read a little young. I liked that they are true to their character. I believe that Percy is twelve despite him having to try and take on challenges that would terrify people many times his age. And the author is consistent with the the trio's skill levels. I just think that I'm not the right person for this book. The mythology is amazing. I love how much Riordan packed in. There's all sorts of gods met and mentioned with places and stories being inserted into the plot all over the place. Journey wise - it didn't feel very planned all the time. Like the trio were sort of stumbling upon where they were supposed to go next. But in the end they got to where they were meant to be so it all worked out for the best I suppose. 
 I'll still watch the movies (provided they make more! Fingers crossed!) but this series isn't for me.

The Percy Jackson series was the first major series I had read; and I was obsessed from the very first word. Needless to say, I'm a big fan of the series. From the hilarious narration from Percy, to the wonderful combination of the modern world and Greek myths, this series was a recipe for goodness from the start. Even now, I am still reading Rick Riordan books. I just can't get enough. The characters he wrote were ( and still are ) memorable and full of heart, and that's hard to write off.
couldn't finish it

Percy Jackson, a troubled dyslexic 12-year-old withADHD, finds out that he is a demigod after some unusual events. He ends up at Camp Half-Blood after his mother takes him to Montauk for the weekend but they get attacked by a Minotaur and she disappears. At the camp, he learns more about life as a demigod, eventually learning that Poseidon is his father. He is sent on a quest to find Zeus's stolen lightning bolt with the help of Grover, a satyr, and Annabeth, a daughter of Athena. The story progresses as expected, adhering strongly to a Hero's Journey storyline with a cliffhanger ending beckoning for the next book in the series. 
 I understand that the series is intensely popular with children, perhaps due to their lack of exposure to better literature. It is incredibly derivative and predictable. The characters are flat, boring and irritating. Percy himself is annoyingly bratty and Riordan spends more time forcefully telling rather than showing Percy's personality. The novel is overall very choppy and disjointed, which really causes the novel to drag on forever. The fight scenes lack any suspense, it is obvious that the kids will succeed with hardly any trouble or loss. There is no question to their eventual triumph as they face each obstacle and that absence of tension bleeds the fun out of what could've have been a wonderful story. 
 Riordan goes for the punchline every time with his allusions and homages to the classical Greek literature, resulting in shallow and trite depictions of the various Gods, Goddesses and spirits. His treatment of the material makes it seem as though even he doesn't believe his story is real, as though the author himself was unable to suspend the disbelief necessary for the novel and it is infectious. Also, why in the world does Athena have children?!?

One thing I liked about listening was hearing someone else pronounce the names for the Greek gods, I just wasn't entirely sure of the pronunciation of some of them which is no big deal when you are reading silently to yourself but becomes a bigger problem when you are reading aloud!

book_b.title: The Sea of Monsters (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #2)

sample_reviews.review_text:
It's been a year since Percy Jackson learned that he is a demigod, the son of his human mother and Poseidon, the Greek God of the sea. On his last day of school, Percy hopes to finish the year without any major disasters and head off to Camp Half Blood, a summer camp for demigods. Unfortunately, trouble has a knack for finding Percy, and he has a run-in with some monsters in gym class. Saved by his friend Annabeth and his classmate Tyson, they escape to camp. 
 Camp Half Blood is not how Percy remembers it. The protective magical boundary of camp is collapsing, monsters are invading the borders, and the camp staff has changed. To make things worse, Percy keeps having dreams about his friend Grover, a satyr on a quest, being in danger. It turns out that Grover has created and "empathy link", allowing him to communicate with Percy from a distance. Between Grover, Hermes, and the Gray Sisters, Percy pieces together clues as to how he can save Camp Half Blood, as well as Grover. Percy's latest quest will take him to the Sea of Monsters, the fabled site of creatures such as Charybdis and the Sirens. In this sequel, Percy will take on old foes and new ones, make new friends, and discover more about his father and family. 
 One of the things I love most about this series is how covertly educational it is! Percy interacts with many characters from Greek mythology and Percy often recalls a quick line or two about the story behind those characters. I recall learning about mythology in grade school and it's fun to revisit those tales. Mention is also given to the works of Greek historians, and I must give kudos to Riordan for making Homer's Odyssey seem interesting! 
 I love how you never know what's going to happen next in this series. Yes, you know something isn't going to be as easy as it initially seems, but you never know who or what to expect! Riordan has a tendency of leading the reader to feel like the worst is over, and then suddenly he throws in another unexpected element. I enjoy guessing what is coming based on context clues (e.g. in book one, when they were at Auntie Em's Garden Emporium and there were tons of horrified looking stone statues- If you know your Greek mythology, you know Medusa is coming!). 
 The only thing that drove me nuts about this book was how oblivious Percy seems to have become. In the first book, he's not well versed in mythology so Annabeth and Grover are often explaining what things are to him. If I suddenly discovered that all of those stories I'd learned in school were in fact real, I'd head home and hit the books to learn as much as I possibly could. I'd also become more aware of my surroundings. Percy, however, seems to have gone home and left his demigod self at Camp Half Blood for the year. He is fully aware of the "mist" and how it keeps humans from perceiving otherworldly things, but allows himself to be fooled by it on multiple occasions. He also requires a great deal of explanation from Annabeth regarding mythological stories. Percy has obviously never heard the quote, "Know thy enemy"! 
 This book is by no means a difficult read. It's obviously geared towards a younger crowd, but adults can definitely enjoy it as well! I'm 23, and I love what I've read thus far! I even went ahead and bought the remainder of the series! This book took me a grand total of two days to read, but part of that was because I couldn't put it down. It's well written, and you have the opportunity to learn more about the key characters and their lives, as well as gain more of the history of Camp Half Blood. 
 This second installment in the Percy Jackson series is exciting and interesting, taking the reader to many new places along the East coast of the United States. If you've got a child, or even if you enjoy a light read yourself, this book is the second installment in a series that has many great elements- adventure, mythology, action and more! Check it out!

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is amazing! It seriously keeps you involved the whole time and there are several different villains to keep your eye on!

** spoiler alert ** 
 **This review is for personal purposes only** 
 This is my least favorite of the HP novels. It takes what I didn't not like about Chamber of Secrets (all the unfair doubt of Harry when he knows the truth)and magnifies it with teenage angst. I thought the plot concept was the weakest of any of the books so far - at least the twist of Ginny being controlled by Voldemort in the Chamber of Secrets was fun and unexpected. It was sad that Sirius died, but I didn't feel much of a connection to him in this book as when he showed up at the end of the 3rd book. I didn't like that he was so focused on just being Harry's friend. I also disliked the plot-line of finding out how cruel Sirius and James were - it ended up ruining their characters for me. Even Lily did not come off great in this novel seeing as she married James after seeing his former behavior. I thought the Occlumency could have been better used, instead of just having Harry give up on closing off his mind and that is what leads him to the Ministry. He should have been tested with it when Voldemort showed up and learned to overcome it. Instead (as you find out in the 6th) Voldemort just blocks him off instead and all those lessons were pointless. 
 One of the few things I did like about this book were the women. Hermione handles Harry so well by being both understanding and firm with him. Ginny also blossomed into a real character this time, instead of just being Ron's shy sister who has a crush on Harry. You find out that she is both funny and fiery, taking notes from both the twins and Ron. And finally, Luna is introduced, who I love. I feel like she really adds a special element to the series. 
 The other part I love about the Order of the Phoenix is Dumbledore's Army. I wish this group would have continued into the 6th book, instead of putting the pressure back on Harry to do all the work. 
 Overall, I hate reading this book. It makes me feel tense from all the anger and angst Harry feels and the plot-line does not feel satisfying. I'll probably skip over it in the future.

I am baffled that this series is so popular. While I think the character qualities have some merit, it is just so terribly written, drawn out, and boring. There are some interesting imaginary things, but what happens with all of them--that is, the plot--stinks. Not to mention, each book is successively darker and sadder than the one which came before. For me, that indicates a dark supernatural power in it far more than the witchcraft and sorcery. Perhaps it is merely the power of good advertising. That is the only reason we know about Jackson Pollack, after all.

 I am just slowly working my way through all the Harry Potter audio books and I have to say, they are so much fun. He really is just atrocious, but none the less it is fun to watch Harry mature and enjoy another year of Hogwart adventures!

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is amazing! It seriously keeps you involved the whole time and there are several different villains to keep your eye on!

** spoiler alert ** 
 **This review is for personal purposes only** 
 This is my least favorite of the HP novels. It takes what I didn't not like about Chamber of Secrets (all the unfair doubt of Harry when he knows the truth)and magnifies it with teenage angst. I thought the plot concept was the weakest of any of the books so far - at least the twist of Ginny being controlled by Voldemort in the Chamber of Secrets was fun and unexpected. It was sad that Sirius died, but I didn't feel much of a connection to him in this book as when he showed up at the end of the 3rd book. I didn't like that he was so focused on just being Harry's friend. I also disliked the plot-line of finding out how cruel Sirius and James were - it ended up ruining their characters for me. Even Lily did not come off great in this novel seeing as she married James after seeing his former behavior. I thought the Occlumency could have been better used, instead of just having Harry give up on closing off his mind and that is what leads him to the Ministry. He should have been tested with it when Voldemort showed up and learned to overcome it. Instead (as you find out in the 6th) Voldemort just blocks him off instead and all those lessons were pointless. 
 One of the few things I did like about this book were the women. Hermione handles Harry so well by being both understanding and firm with him. Ginny also blossomed into a real character this time, instead of just being Ron's shy sister who has a crush on Harry. You find out that she is both funny and fiery, taking notes from both the twins and Ron. And finally, Luna is introduced, who I love. I feel like she really adds a special element to the series. 
 The other part I love about the Order of the Phoenix is Dumbledore's Army. I wish this group would have continued into the 6th book, instead of putting the pressure back on Harry to do all the work. 
 Overall, I hate reading this book. It makes me feel tense from all the anger and angst Harry feels and the plot-line does not feel satisfying. I'll probably skip over it in the future.

I am baffled that this series is so popular. While I think the character qualities have some merit, it is just so terribly written, drawn out, and boring. There are some interesting imaginary things, but what happens with all of them--that is, the plot--stinks. Not to mention, each book is successively darker and sadder than the one which came before. For me, that indicates a dark supernatural power in it far more than the witchcraft and sorcery. Perhaps it is merely the power of good advertising. That is the only reason we know about Jackson Pollack, after all.

book_a.title: The Battle of the Labyrinth (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #4)

sample_reviews.review_text:
The Battle Of The Labyrinth (Percy Jackson And The Olympians #4), by Rick Riordan 
 Synopsis: Percy Jackson isn't expecting freshman orientation to be any fun. But when a mysterious mortal acquaintance appears on campus, followed by demon cheerleaders, things quickly move from bad to worse. 
 In this fourth installment of the blockbuster series, time is running out as war between the Olympians and the evil Titan lord Kronos draws near. Even the safe haven of Camp Half-Blood grows more vulnerable by the minute as Kronos's army prepares to invade its once impenetrable borders. To stop the invasion, Percy and his demigod friends must set out on a quest through the Labyrinth - a sprawling underground world with stunning surprises at every turn. 
 In A Sentence: A decent read, but I'm not feeling very wowed by this series (not yet anyway) 
 My Thoughts: At this point I admit I'm starting to just power through the series. It's a fun series that kids and young adults would really enjoy, but as an adult I don't feel as wowed as I could be. The chapter titles still pull a chuckle out of me, and there are sentences peppered throughout the story that are also pretty funny (case in point: "You hit the Lord of the Titans in the eye with a blue plastic hairbrush"). Ridiculous scenarios seem to be the main trademark of these books, which is always fun, but beyond that, the story doesn't hold a whole lot of depth. It's your typical action novels: lots of energy and a fast-paced plot, but very little depth and complexity. 
 Would I recommend this read? Of course! It's easy-going fun that doesn't require too much concentration. It's ridiculously funny in parts, and the incorporation of Greek Mythology into today's world is loads of fun to read about. Plus, it's a fast read, perfect for your next vacation. I'm starting the final book now and I'm looking forward to seeing how it ends. Happy reading!

Harry Potter. Everyone has at least heard of the story. This is actually my third time reading the book, and I have to say after reading so many children's books, I can see what it has taken the world by storm. 
 Harry Potter is orphaned as a baby and send to live with his terrible uncle and aunt, the Dursleys. His cousin, Dudley, is the same age as Harry, and bullies him. Harry's bedroom is the tiny room under the stairs, meanwhile, Dudley has two bedrooms, one to sleep in and one for all of his toys! This is the life that Harry has lived for the past ten years. Then one day a letter arrives for him, but instead of being allowed to read it, his uncle keeps them from Harry. But there is no escape. A giant, named Hagrid shows up and explains to Harry what his aunt and uncle have been hiding; Harry is a wizard! 
 Next thing Harry knows he is off to a special school where he finally makes friends. He also has some enemies, but for the first time in his life, he feels like he belongs. I love the way this book is written. There is humor and creativity. Harry finds himself in one adventure after another, and he also learns what it is like to have people care for you. Great book that really will appeal to all ages, not just the target audience of a middle grade reader.

I feel like this book killed my brain cells.

I've seen the movies and loved them so I thought it was about time I saw where everything began for Percy, Grover and Annabeth. The Lightning Thief by Rick Riordan tells the story of how twelve year old Percy Jackson discovers he's a demigod. Son of Poseidon, Percy has never quite been like other kids. If Percy is to find the bolt (and consequentially save his mother and become a hero) - he needs to overcome monsters and battle gods. Not alone in his quest, his best friend Grover and one of Athena's daughters, Annabeth, tag along to give Percy the best chance against the powerful immortals. 
 For the right audience, I believe this book would be perfect. There's action and adventure. A great take on classic mythology and characters I could fall in love with. 
 The problem is - I'm not the right audience. I'm in my twenties and unlike a lot of other young adult and middle grade books I've read - this one made me feel old in a way no other book I've read before has. 
 The characters, as entertaining as they are, read a little young. I liked that they are true to their character. I believe that Percy is twelve despite him having to try and take on challenges that would terrify people many times his age. And the author is consistent with the the trio's skill levels. I just think that I'm not the right person for this book. The mythology is amazing. I love how much Riordan packed in. There's all sorts of gods met and mentioned with places and stories being inserted into the plot all over the place. Journey wise - it didn't feel very planned all the time. Like the trio were sort of stumbling upon where they were supposed to go next. But in the end they got to where they were meant to be so it all worked out for the best I suppose.

I liked it but I wasn't so into it like Harry Potter. I think boys would really enjoy it and it's not as scary or dark as Harry Potter.

couldn't finish it

For many, these series of books are considered to be a Harry Potter rip-off but in reality they are just following the established formula of all teen/children adventures. So it is a fine book at what it's all about but hardly feels special if you have read or watched enough of the same type. 
 So, as the stereotype dictates, the hero is a boy who is treated at first as a looser before he is revealed to be the son of a God and taken to train to a special school of half-breeds just like him. Throw in some basic Greek mythology, lots of monsters, some conspiracy that can destroy the world, and there you go, you get the much familiar path Harry Potter made famous but otherwise did not establish. 
 Just like most such stories, it suffers from what I call "weakened enemies". Since he is constantly fighting monsters and rivals gods, you would expect for him to be some epic-level fighter who does all sorts of stuff but all you see is an everyday boy who can hardly manage at school. It makes all the challenges he faces to pass as pathetic if any kid can beat up a Minotaur with a few sword swings or a Hydra with a hax Medusa head. I am pretty sure most of the target audience won't notice or even care about that, as it feels very cool if a nobody can do all those cool stuff. Yeah, I wonder how many of them realize that this nobody is a demigod who is constantly aided by all sorts of people and other gods just because he was born special. 
 The second thing it suffers from is how the plot seems to drive him and not him driving the plot as it would normally be the case. He is just running from one mission to another without really deciding anything for himself, or even accomplishing anything with his own strength or cunningness. Heck, even I could rival the gods if had for free all the allies and equipment he gets. Just think of all the main events he was part of. 
 - Fending off the Fury because someone intervened. 
 - Accused of being a thief without having a saying in the whole thing. 
 - Fending off the Minotaur because of a magic sword someone else gave him. 
 - Taken to the training camp without choosing it. 
 - Finding a way to save his mother through someone else, whom he didn't even ask for help. 
 - Beating the Medusa with a pitiful excuse. 
 - Beating Hades without really fighting him. He was betrayed. 
 - Fighting the real villain with the powers his father gave him. 
 So he feels too much like a plot device instead of a boy who tries to fight his destiny or something like that. He never even questions his own status but rather runs after the more experienced ones. 
 The third problem is the villain of the book, rather easy to tell who it's going to be despite being hidden. The main conflict of the book also makes no sense at all. If the lightning bolt was so powerful and precious, how was it stolen so easily by a nobody? How can anyone blame Percy as the thief when he never went to the temple of the gods or didn't even know they exist? If the villain knew how to go to the underworld, why didn't he just go there himself? And what a classic, when revealed he just explains his plan in detail, as if it matters at all to someone he plans on killing a few minutes later. 
 The fourth problem is quite minor if you are not Greek. I am and I found all this bastardization of my country's mythology rather insulting. All of a sudden the whole realm of the gods is at some American soil and the three main gods are rivals. Oh come on! 
 But I guess it is a fine line of books for kids since the plot is rather fast and it has magic and monsters and gods and stuff happening every few pages. Cool but hardly great.

Yeah that didn't happen, I think altogether I got started on the third book then something shiny caught my eye and so I never finished and that's kind of where I left Percy Jackson. 
 I am appallingly bad at finishing series however audiobooks are serving me very well right now and they did wonders to Harry Potter for me so I bought the first two audiobooks of Percy Jackson which are read by a gentleman called Jesse Bernstein which I first heard him I was convinced that he was the voice of Spongebob but turns out no. 
 (I have absolutely no idea what made me think that.) 
 He is one of those grown men who can make himself still sound like a teenager so considering the books are told through through Percys point of view is a pretty decent fit. Although the deep voices he does for the villain and the gods don't really work. 
 My opinion of the actual story is still the same. Brilliant. All Greek gods did was mess around with humans and make little Demi-Gods so why wouldn't they still be doing that in modern times? Riordan has managed to make Greek Mythology which was the worlds first R rated soap opera friendly for kids without dumbing it down so kudos for that. 
 At this point it doesn't have as much depth as the Harry Potter books did with the story but early days. I'm enjoying this a lot and will be purchasing the other books to listen to.

I don't know if it was all the hoopla I've heard about this that built it up too much in my head, or what. I closed the book with a shrug of the shoulders and a "meh" on my lips, feeling resoundingly underwhelmed. i started reading it to my somewhat timid 9 yo son. The only plus I can see from reading it is that I now have a better grasp of who some of the Greek gods are. So there's something at least! I'm still undecided if I will finish the series or not.

book_b.title: The Battle of the Labyrinth (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #4)

sample_reviews.review_text:
The Battle Of The Labyrinth (Percy Jackson And The Olympians #4), by Rick Riordan 
 Synopsis: Percy Jackson isn't expecting freshman orientation to be any fun. But when a mysterious mortal acquaintance appears on campus, followed by demon cheerleaders, things quickly move from bad to worse. 
 In this fourth installment of the blockbuster series, time is running out as war between the Olympians and the evil Titan lord Kronos draws near. Even the safe haven of Camp Half-Blood grows more vulnerable by the minute as Kronos's army prepares to invade its once impenetrable borders. To stop the invasion, Percy and his demigod friends must set out on a quest through the Labyrinth - a sprawling underground world with stunning surprises at every turn. 
 In A Sentence: A decent read, but I'm not feeling very wowed by this series (not yet anyway) 
 My Thoughts: At this point I admit I'm starting to just power through the series. It's a fun series that kids and young adults would really enjoy, but as an adult I don't feel as wowed as I could be. The chapter titles still pull a chuckle out of me, and there are sentences peppered throughout the story that are also pretty funny (case in point: "You hit the Lord of the Titans in the eye with a blue plastic hairbrush"). Ridiculous scenarios seem to be the main trademark of these books, which is always fun, but beyond that, the story doesn't hold a whole lot of depth. It's your typical action novels: lots of energy and a fast-paced plot, but very little depth and complexity. 
 Would I recommend this read? Of course! It's easy-going fun that doesn't require too much concentration. It's ridiculously funny in parts, and the incorporation of Greek Mythology into today's world is loads of fun to read about. Plus, it's a fast read, perfect for your next vacation. I'm starting the final book now and I'm looking forward to seeing how it ends. Happy reading!

Personally I believe dream sequences are a lazy crutch authors use when they can't think of a way to logically advance part of the story.

Hidden in the mortal world to protect him from those with grudges against his biological father, Percy has always known that he was different. When Zeus' lightning bolt is stolen, Percy's existence comes to light and his paternity is revealed. If Percy is to find the bolt (and consequentially save his mother and become a hero) - he needs to overcome monsters and battle gods. Not alone in his quest, his best friend Grover and one of Athena's daughters, Annabeth, tag along to give Percy the best chance against the powerful immortals. 
 For the right audience, I believe this book would be perfect. There's action and adventure. A great take on classic mythology and characters I could fall in love with. 
 The problem is - I'm not the right audience. I'm in my twenties and unlike a lot of other young adult and middle grade books I've read - this one made me feel old in a way no other book I've read before has. 
 The characters, as entertaining as they are, read a little young. I liked that they are true to their character. I believe that Percy is twelve despite him having to try and take on challenges that would terrify people many times his age. And the author is consistent with the the trio's skill levels. I just think that I'm not the right person for this book. The mythology is amazing. I love how much Riordan packed in. There's all sorts of gods met and mentioned with places and stories being inserted into the plot all over the place. Journey wise - it didn't feel very planned all the time. Like the trio were sort of stumbling upon where they were supposed to go next. But in the end they got to where they were meant to be so it all worked out for the best I suppose. 
 I'll still watch the movies (provided they make more! Fingers crossed!) but this series isn't for me.
I liked it but I wasn't so into it like Harry Potter. I think boys would really enjoy it and it's not as scary or dark as Harry Potter.

For many, these series of books are considered to be a Harry Potter rip-off but in reality they are just following the established formula of all teen/children adventures. So it is a fine book at what it's all about but hardly feels special if you have read or watched enough of the same type. 
 So, as the stereotype dictates, the hero is a boy who is treated at first as a looser before he is revealed to be the son of a God and taken to train to a special school of half-breeds just like him. Throw in some basic Greek mythology, lots of monsters, some conspiracy that can destroy the world, and there you go, you get the much familiar path Harry Potter made famous but otherwise did not establish. 
 Just like most such stories, it suffers from what I call "weakened enemies". Since he is constantly fighting monsters and rivals gods, you would expect for him to be some epic-level fighter who does all sorts of stuff but all you see is an everyday boy who can hardly manage at school. It makes all the challenges he faces to pass as pathetic if any kid can beat up a Minotaur with a few sword swings or a Hydra with a hax Medusa head. I am pretty sure most of the target audience won't notice or even care about that, as it feels very cool if a nobody can do all those cool stuff. Yeah, I wonder how many of them realize that this nobody is a demigod who is constantly aided by all sorts of people and other gods just because he was born special. 
 The second thing it suffers from is how the plot seems to drive him and not him driving the plot as it would normally be the case. He is just running from one mission to another without really deciding anything for himself, or even accomplishing anything with his own strength or cunningness. Heck, even I could rival the gods if had for free all the allies and equipment he gets. Just think of all the main events he was part of. 
 - Fending off the Fury because someone intervened. 
 - Accused of being a thief without having a saying in the whole thing. 
 - Fending off the Minotaur because of a magic sword someone else gave him. 
 - Taken to the training camp without choosing it. 
 - Finding a way to save his mother through someone else, whom he didn't even ask for help. 
 - Beating the Medusa with a pitiful excuse. 
 - Beating Hades without really fighting him. He was betrayed. 
 - Fighting the real villain with the powers his father gave him. 
 So he feels too much like a plot device instead of a boy who tries to fight his destiny or something like that. He never even questions his own status but rather runs after the more experienced ones. 
 The third problem is the villain of the book, rather easy to tell who it's going to be despite being hidden. The main conflict of the book also makes no sense at all. If the lightning bolt was so powerful and precious, how was it stolen so easily by a nobody? How can anyone blame Percy as the thief when he never went to the temple of the gods or didn't even know they exist? If the villain knew how to go to the underworld, why didn't he just go there himself? And what a classic, when revealed he just explains his plan in detail, as if it matters at all to someone he plans on killing a few minutes later. 
 The fourth problem is quite minor if you are not Greek. I am and I found all this bastardization of my country's mythology rather insulting. All of a sudden the whole realm of the gods is at some American soil and the three main gods are rivals. Oh come on! 
 But I guess it is a fine line of books for kids since the plot is rather fast and it has magic and monsters and gods and stuff happening every few pages. Cool but hardly great.

 I am appallingly bad at finishing series however audiobooks are serving me very well right now and they did wonders to Harry Potter for me so I bought the first two audiobooks of Percy Jackson which are read by a gentleman called Jesse Bernstein which I first heard him I was convinced that he was the voice of Spongebob but turns out no.

Riordan has managed to make Greek Mythology which was the worlds first R rated soap opera friendly for kids without dumbing it down so kudos for that.

sample_reviews.review_text:
The Battle Of The Labyrinth (Percy Jackson And The Olympians #4), by Rick Riordan 
 Synopsis: Percy Jackson isn't expecting freshman orientation to be any fun. But when a mysterious mortal acquaintance appears on campus, followed by demon cheerleaders, things quickly move from bad to worse. 
 In this fourth installment of the blockbuster series, time is running out as war between the Olympians and the evil Titan lord Kronos draws near. Even the safe haven of Camp Half-Blood grows more vulnerable by the minute as Kronos's army prepares to invade its once impenetrable borders. To stop the invasion, Percy and his demigod friends must set out on a quest through the Labyrinth - a sprawling underground world with stunning surprises at every turn. 
 In A Sentence: A decent read, but I'm not feeling very wowed by this series (not yet anyway) 
 My Thoughts: At this point I admit I'm starting to just power through the series. It's a fun series that kids and young adults would really enjoy, but as an adult I don't feel as wowed as I could be. The chapter titles still pull a chuckle out of me, and there are sentences peppered throughout the story that are also pretty funny (case in point: "You hit the Lord of the Titans in the eye with a blue plastic hairbrush"). Ridiculous scenarios seem to be the main trademark of these books, which is always fun, but beyond that, the story doesn't hold a whole lot of depth. It's your typical action novels: lots of energy and a fast-paced plot, but very little depth and complexity. 
 Would I recommend this read? Of course! It's easy-going fun that doesn't require too much concentration. It's ridiculously funny in parts, and the incorporation of Greek Mythology into today's world is loads of fun to read about. Plus, it's a fast read, perfect for your next vacation. I'm starting the final book now and I'm looking forward to seeing how it ends. Happy reading!

Harry Potter. Everyone has at least heard of the story. This is actually my third time reading the book, and I have to say after reading so many children's books, I can see what it has taken the world by storm. 
 Harry Potter is orphaned as a baby and send to live with his terrible uncle and aunt, the Dursleys. His cousin, Dudley, is the same age as Harry, and bullies him. Harry's bedroom is the tiny room under the stairs, meanwhile, Dudley has two bedrooms, one to sleep in and one for all of his toys! This is the life that Harry has lived for the past ten years. Then one day a letter arrives for him, but instead of being allowed to read it, his uncle keeps them from Harry. But there is no escape. A giant, named Hagrid shows up and explains to Harry what his aunt and uncle have been hiding; Harry is a wizard! 
 Next thing Harry knows he is off to a special school where he finally makes friends. He also has some enemies, but for the first time in his life, he feels like he belongs. I love the way this book is written. There is humor and creativity. Harry finds himself in one adventure after another, and he also learns what it is like to have people care for you. Great book that really will appeal to all ages, not just the target audience of a middle grade reader.

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is amazing! It seriously keeps you involved the whole time and there are several different villains to keep your eye on!

** spoiler alert ** 
 **This review is for personal purposes only** 
 This is my least favorite of the HP novels. It takes what I didn't not like about Chamber of Secrets (all the unfair doubt of Harry when he knows the truth)and magnifies it with teenage angst. I thought the plot concept was the weakest of any of the books so far - at least the twist of Ginny being controlled by Voldemort in the Chamber of Secrets was fun and unexpected. It was sad that Sirius died, but I didn't feel much of a connection to him in this book as when he showed up at the end of the 3rd book. I didn't like that he was so focused on just being Harry's friend. I also disliked the plot-line of finding out how cruel Sirius and James were - it ended up ruining their characters for me. Even Lily did not come off great in this novel seeing as she married James after seeing his former behavior. I thought the Occlumency could have been better used, instead of just having Harry give up on closing off his mind and that is what leads him to the Ministry. He should have been tested with it when Voldemort showed up and learned to overcome it. Instead (as you find out in the 6th) Voldemort just blocks him off instead and all those lessons were pointless. 
 One of the few things I did like about this book were the women. Hermione handles Harry so well by being both understanding and firm with him. Ginny also blossomed into a real character this time, instead of just being Ron's shy sister who has a crush on Harry. You find out that she is both funny and fiery, taking notes from both the twins and Ron. And finally, Luna is introduced, who I love. I feel like she really adds a special element to the series. 
 The other part I love about the Order of the Phoenix is Dumbledore's Army. I wish this group would have continued into the 6th book, instead of putting the pressure back on Harry to do all the work. 
 Overall, I hate reading this book. It makes me feel tense from all the anger and angst Harry feels and the plot-line does not feel satisfying. I'll probably skip over it in the future.

So much of the expert advice on writing is about advancing the plot, moving the story ahead, cutting out unnecessary detail. Harry Potter 5 breaks those rules, and it's a better book for it. 
 All this is old news, but I re-read most of The Order of The Phoenix over the holidays, just because I like it so much. And also because I appreciate its brief but gentle treatment of mental illness. 
 My absolute favorite scene is when Neville, a minor character, realizes his friends know that his parents are mentally ill. His bossy grandmother is there, and she tells him what to do and how to feel. But Neville takes his own approach, which is shyer, sweeter and in the end much more courageous. 
 Another wonderful minor character was the socially awkward Luna Lovegood. My favorite scene with her is at the very end of the book, when Harry stumbles onto Luna in the hall on the last day of the term. At first he wants to hide from her. Then, when he realizes that she knows how odd she seems to everyone else, he feels sorry for her. By the time he walks away, he is very glad to have talked to her. 
 I thought it was sad when Luna told Harry that their schoolmates played tricks on her. Bret disagreed. "She wasn't sad about it," he said. "She was handling it just fine." 
 And she was--which may explain why her strangeness is so likable. 
 She and the clumsy but determined Neville are the reasons I've read Harry Potter 5 more than once.

2017 reread. I remember being disappointed in this ending. It was worth 3 stars then, and I'm giving it 4 now. 
 I think the difference is me, and what point in life I read it. Some fundamental issues I had with the book were more about me, my life experiences at the time, and I was fairly exhausted and impatient generally in 2007. 
 For example, I hated the Dumbledore scenes, but now I don't. I hated the resolution, and now I don't. Maybe I've just had time to sit with the ideas, or maybe the straight through reread made it so much deeper for me. I'm not sure. 
 I still feel it's unevenly paced, and I do wish there had been equal time to the last half of the book as the first. I wish we could have seen more of Hogwarts, had a clue what was going on with DA and Snape. The wand stuff really seems spotty, still. But generally, it's a much more satisfying resolution to the story than I remember. 
 On to The Cursed Child!

book_a.title: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (Harry Potter, #3)

sample_reviews.review_text: My favorite HP book forever!

A wizard criminal named Sirius Black has escaped from the top-security prison, Azkaban, and all signs point to him targeting Harry Potter. The soul-sucking guardians of the prison, the Dementors, are installed at Hogwarts to protect the students, but they're much more of a disruption than a comfort. Harry, Hermione, and Ron experience speed bumps in their friendship due to squabbles over whether Hermione's cat ate Ron's rat and Hermione reporting a mysterious gift that Harry received (presumably for his own protection). But the trio are all united in trying to save Buckbeak, Hagrid's hippogriff, who is due to be executed because he hurt a nasty student who provoked him. But when Ron's rat does turn out to be somewhere--and someONE--that he'd never suspected, other old friends come out of the woodwork, including Sirius Black himself. But exactly whose side is Sirius on--and who are his allies? It could very well be that Harry may finally learn a few things about his family. 
 The Dementors are a horrifying idea. They were expertly handled as an eerie presence in the book, though I had trouble imagining any grand wizarding society would accept their widespread use for the cause of order when they can suck people's souls out. I liked the switcharoo of loyalties and the way the characters' pets figured in, but I again got frustrated at how nobody tells Harry anything for the sake of a nifty reveal at the end. The red herrings are kind of out of control sometimes.

What an amazing journey! I almost cried.almost.

 "I solemnly swear that I am up to no good."

I found myself getting really annoyed with Harry's "special one" treatment in this book. I get that he's the main character and he has to be special, but everyone treats him like he's the Second Coming, and it started to get old in this book. I actually thought Snape made some good points, that Harry thinks he can get away with anything and the rules don't apply to him. It's totally true. Even Dumbledore makes a fool of Snape in front of Harry. It seemed very unprofessional of him to me. If he doesn't want Snape teaching there, he shouldn't have hired him! I really didn't like how everyone catered to Harry, and how, yet again, Harry manages to ditch his friends to be the lone hero and defeat the bad guys all by himself at the end. It would be nice if his friends could contribute to the climactic fight scene in ONE of the books and show some themes about friendship and such. Just my two cents. I didn't love this one at all.

book_b.title: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (Harry Potter, #5)

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is amazing! It seriously keeps you involved the whole time and there are several different villains to keep your eye on!

** spoiler alert ** 
 **This review is for personal purposes only** 
 This is my least favorite of the HP novels. It takes what I didn't not like about Chamber of Secrets (all the unfair doubt of Harry when he knows the truth)and magnifies it with teenage angst. I thought the plot concept was the weakest of any of the books so far - at least the twist of Ginny being controlled by Voldemort in the Chamber of Secrets was fun and unexpected. It was sad that Sirius died, but I didn't feel much of a connection to him in this book as when he showed up at the end of the 3rd book. I didn't like that he was so focused on just being Harry's friend. I also disliked the plot-line of finding out how cruel Sirius and James were - it ended up ruining their characters for me. Even Lily did not come off great in this novel seeing as she married James after seeing his former behavior. I thought the Occlumency could have been better used, instead of just having Harry give up on closing off his mind and that is what leads him to the Ministry. He should have been tested with it when Voldemort showed up and learned to overcome it. Instead (as you find out in the 6th) Voldemort just blocks him off instead and all those lessons were pointless. 
 One of the few things I did like about this book were the women. Hermione handles Harry so well by being both understanding and firm with him. Ginny also blossomed into a real character this time, instead of just being Ron's shy sister who has a crush on Harry. You find out that she is both funny and fiery, taking notes from both the twins and Ron. And finally, Luna is introduced, who I love. I feel like she really adds a special element to the series. 
 The other part I love about the Order of the Phoenix is Dumbledore's Army. I wish this group would have continued into the 6th book, instead of putting the pressure back on Harry to do all the work. 
 Overall, I hate reading this book. It makes me feel tense from all the anger and angst Harry feels and the plot-line does not feel satisfying. I'll probably skip over it in the future.

I am baffled that this series is so popular. While I think the character qualities have some merit, it is just so terribly written, drawn out, and boring. There are some interesting imaginary things, but what happens with all of them--that is, the plot--stinks. Not to mention, each book is successively darker and sadder than the one which came before. For me, that indicates a dark supernatural power in it far more than the witchcraft and sorcery. Perhaps it is merely the power of good advertising. That is the only reason we know about Jackson Pollack, after all.
:D

As much as I love Rowling, I didn't enjoy this book as much as I would've wanted to. I also started this book in December then due to school I wasn't able to pick it back up again until June making it a little hard to get back into the groove of reading this book. I felt as though the book moved along slowly for me and it didn't start picking up until the last 6 chapters, where I found myself unable to put the book down until I finished it. If I had that feeling during the beginning or even during the halfway point of the book then I would have easily given this book a 4 out of 5 or even a 5 out of 5. Instead, due to the slow lag I could only give the book a 3. Also, Harry's attitude was slightly annoying to me as well during the middle half of the book. He would get angry and yell and just plainly be rude with the only people willing to help him in a dire situation. I love Luna Lovegood and wished that she was more prominent in this book. Hopefully, she'll get more shine as the series progresses.

Rowling is such an amazing writer, with so much description. It just takes me SOOO long to read 870 pages.

So much of the expert advice on writing is about advancing the plot, moving the story ahead, cutting out unnecessary detail. Harry Potter 5 breaks those rules, and it's a better book for it. 
 All this is old news, but I re-read most of The Order of The Phoenix over the holidays, just because I like it so much. And also because I appreciate its brief but gentle treatment of mental illness. 
 My absolute favorite scene is when Neville, a minor character, realizes his friends know that his parents are mentally ill. His bossy grandmother is there, and she tells him what to do and how to feel. But Neville takes his own approach, which is shyer, sweeter and in the end much more courageous. 
 Another wonderful minor character was the socially awkward Luna Lovegood. My favorite scene with her is at the very end of the book, when Harry stumbles onto Luna in the hall on the last day of the term. At first he wants to hide from her. Then, when he realizes that she knows how odd she seems to everyone else, he feels sorry for her. By the time he walks away, he is very glad to have talked to her. 
 I thought it was sad when Luna told Harry that their schoolmates played tricks on her. Bret disagreed. "She wasn't sad about it," he said. "She was handling it just fine." 
 And she was--which may explain why her strangeness is so likable. 
 She and the clumsy but determined Neville are the reasons I've read Harry Potter 5 more than once.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Short and Sweet Review, by Michelle: 
 Ahh, all good things must come to an end. I am a Harry Potter nut. Why the three stars then? Well, I don't know to be honest with you. I "liked it", but I just don't know if I can go further than that. Maybe 3.5 stars? What really ruined the book for me was the epilogue. Had Ms. Rowling not included the epilogue, I think I could have gone with 4 stars. It just felt so cheesy after all the darkness that we've experienced throughout the development of the story. 
 Eh, well, I think that's all I really need to say. I highly doubt someone is scouring reviews of Harry Potter to decide if they're going to read it or not. ;) So I'll keep in short & sweet, per usual!
Amazing!!!
I was probably the last of my generation to read this book. It's fantastic. I cried and books don't ever make me cry. Stayed up all night reading it like a little kid. Whatever.

Bittersweet Book. It is an amazing and emotional conclusion to the journey we started 7 years prior. Sadly, we must let go of the characters, at least for now. Rowling brings in the epic-ness for one final showdown. No one is forgotten. Every character gets some form of a conclusion, only leaving questions for us fangirls/boys about their futures beyond. This is by the best of the series. Full 5 out of 5 stars, although should be more in possible. Nothing more to say, other than, if you haven't read this series yet, why are you reading this, go now, in any way you choose, discover the wonderful world of Harry Potter.

2017 reread. I remember being disappointed in this ending. It was worth 3 stars then, and I'm giving it 4 now. 
 I think the difference is me, and what point in life I read it. Some fundamental issues I had with the book were more about me, my life experiences at the time, and I was fairly exhausted and impatient generally in 2007. 
 For example, I hated the Dumbledore scenes, but now I don't. I hated the resolution, and now I don't. Maybe I've just had time to sit with the ideas, or maybe the straight through reread made it so much deeper for me. I'm not sure. 
 I still feel it's unevenly paced, and I do wish there had been equal time to the last half of the book as the first. I wish we could have seen more of Hogwarts, had a clue what was going on with DA and Snape. The wand stuff really seems spotty, still. But generally, it's a much more satisfying resolution to the story than I remember. 
 On to The Cursed Child!
Sad that the series is ending, happy because Voldy is gone, and estatic that Ron and Hermione and Harry and Ginny get together. It's all mixed feelings.

give me back my life damnit, I could have done without 500 pages of the book. Wish I had gone with my initial instinct and just checked for a detailed synopsis. Thank goodness for the couple of scenes that did end up finishing the series nicely, but give me lloyd alexander any day over this. The series would have been much better if 5,6, and 7 had been consolidated into one reasonably sized book.
Re-read December 2016
Rating 2.5 (Please don't flame me)

book_a.title: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (Harry Potter, #5)

sample_reviews.review_text: This book is amazing! It seriously keeps you involved the whole time and there are several different villains to keep your eye on!

** spoiler alert ** 
 **This review is for personal purposes only** 
 This is my least favorite of the HP novels. It takes what I didn't not like about Chamber of Secrets (all the unfair doubt of Harry when he knows the truth)and magnifies it with teenage angst. I thought the plot concept was the weakest of any of the books so far - at least the twist of Ginny being controlled by Voldemort in the Chamber of Secrets was fun and unexpected. It was sad that Sirius died, but I didn't feel much of a connection to him in this book as when he showed up at the end of the 3rd book. I didn't like that he was so focused on just being Harry's friend. I also disliked the plot-line of finding out how cruel Sirius and James were - it ended up ruining their characters for me. Even Lily did not come off great in this novel seeing as she married James after seeing his former behavior. I thought the Occlumency could have been better used, instead of just having Harry give up on closing off his mind and that is what leads him to the Ministry. He should have been tested with it when Voldemort showed up and learned to overcome it. Instead (as you find out in the 6th) Voldemort just blocks him off instead and all those lessons were pointless. 
 One of the few things I did like about this book were the women. Hermione handles Harry so well by being both understanding and firm with him. Ginny also blossomed into a real character this time, instead of just being Ron's shy sister who has a crush on Harry. You find out that she is both funny and fiery, taking notes from both the twins and Ron. And finally, Luna is introduced, who I love. I feel like she really adds a special element to the series. 
 The other part I love about the Order of the Phoenix is Dumbledore's Army. I wish this group would have continued into the 6th book, instead of putting the pressure back on Harry to do all the work. 
 Overall, I hate reading this book. It makes me feel tense from all the anger and angst Harry feels and the plot-line does not feel satisfying. I'll probably skip over it in the future.

I am baffled that this series is so popular. While I think the character qualities have some merit, it is just so terribly written, drawn out, and boring. There are some interesting imaginary things, but what happens with all of them--that is, the plot--stinks. Not to mention, each book is successively darker and sadder than the one which came before. For me, that indicates a dark supernatural power in it far more than the witchcraft and sorcery. Perhaps it is merely the power of good advertising. That is the only reason we know about Jackson Pollack, after all.

So much of the expert advice on writing is about advancing the plot, moving the story ahead, cutting out unnecessary detail. Harry Potter 5 breaks those rules, and it's a better book for it. 
 All this is old news, but I re-read most of The Order of The Phoenix over the holidays, just because I like it so much. And also because I appreciate its brief but gentle treatment of mental illness. 
 My absolute favorite scene is when Neville, a minor character, realizes his friends know that his parents are mentally ill. His bossy grandmother is there, and she tells him what to do and how to feel. But Neville takes his own approach, which is shyer, sweeter and in the end much more courageous. 
 Another wonderful minor character was the socially awkward Luna Lovegood. My favorite scene with her is at the very end of the book, when Harry stumbles onto Luna in the hall on the last day of the term. At first he wants to hide from her. Then, when he realizes that she knows how odd she seems to everyone else, he feels sorry for her. By the time he walks away, he is very glad to have talked to her. 
 I thought it was sad when Luna told Harry that their schoolmates played tricks on her. Bret disagreed. "She wasn't sad about it," he said. "She was handling it just fine." 
 And she was--which may explain why her strangeness is so likable. 
 She and the clumsy but determined Neville are the reasons I've read Harry Potter 5 more than once.

sample_reviews.review_text:
Short and Sweet Review, by Michelle: 
 Ahh, all good things must come to an end. I am a Harry Potter nut. Why the three stars then? Well, I don't know to be honest with you. I "liked it", but I just don't know if I can go further than that. Maybe 3.5 stars? What really ruined the book for me was the epilogue. Had Ms. Rowling not included the epilogue, I think I could have gone with 4 stars. It just felt so cheesy after all the darkness that we've experienced throughout the development of the story. 
 Eh, well, I think that's all I really need to say. I highly doubt someone is scouring reviews of Harry Potter to decide if they're going to read it or not. ;) So I'll keep in short & sweet, per usual!
Amazing!!!
I was probably the last of my generation to read this book. It's fantastic. I cried and books don't ever make me cry. Stayed up all night reading it like a little kid. Whatever.

Bittersweet Book. It is an amazing and emotional conclusion to the journey we started 7 years prior. Sadly, we must let go of the characters, at least for now. Rowling brings in the epic-ness for one final showdown. No one is forgotten. Every character gets some form of a conclusion, only leaving questions for us fangirls/boys about their futures beyond. This is by the best of the series. Full 5 out of 5 stars, although should be more in possible. Nothing more to say, other than, if you haven't read this series yet, why are you reading this, go now, in any way you choose, discover the wonderful world of Harry Potter.

2017 reread. I remember being disappointed in this ending. It was worth 3 stars then, and I'm giving it 4 now. 
 I think the difference is me, and what point in life I read it. Some fundamental issues I had with the book were more about me, my life experiences at the time, and I was fairly exhausted and impatient generally in 2007. 
 For example, I hated the Dumbledore scenes, but now I don't. I hated the resolution, and now I don't. Maybe I've just had time to sit with the ideas, or maybe the straight through reread made it so much deeper for me. I'm not sure. 
 I still feel it's unevenly paced, and I do wish there had been equal time to the last half of the book as the first. I wish we could have seen more of Hogwarts, had a clue what was going on with DA and Snape. The wand stuff really seems spotty, still. But generally, it's a much more satisfying resolution to the story than I remember. 
 On to The Cursed Child!
Sad that the series is ending, happy because Voldy is gone, and estatic that Ron and Hermione and Harry and Ginny get together. It's all mixed feelings.

book_a.title: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (Harry Potter, #4)

sample_reviews.review_text:
OMG. I'm once again dumped head first into the world of Harry Potter. 
 I absolutely love how JK Rowling feeds us a bit of information and it turns out to be useful in the end. Nothing goes to waste and nothing is without purpose. GoF is more action based than it's precedents and things really go up a notch. Now, we really see the reality of being Harry Potter hit him. Before this, while it isn't always nice, it's a lot of fanfare and roses. I saw this thing on Tumble saying how in books 1-3, Harry is all like 'Fuck yeah! I'm Harry Potter!' and in books 4-6, he's like 'Fuck, I'm Harry Potter.' HHahahhaa that's really accurate.
Reread December 2016. Still as exciting and heartbreaking and incredible as ever.

I know a lot of people that think this book is one of the worst of the series. Worst being a loosely used term considering it's Harry Potter. Kind of like how Temple of Doom is considered the worst Indiana Jones movie, but it's still awesome because it's Indiana Jones. Anyway, those people are insane in the membrane. 
 Goblet of Fire is where things start to get truly awesome. The first three books in the series follow a pretty rigid formula: pre-Hogwarts -> at Hogwarts -> Malfoy is annoy/classes are almost a sidenote -> harry & co find out something sinister is going on -> investigation while dealing with quidditch worries -> reveal -> Harry stops Voldemort from coming back -> everyone smiles. Goblet of Fire, while loosely following that same formula, breaks free of the restrictions and does something different. Quidditch is replaced with the Triwizard tournament and sh!t is just straight cray-cray for Harry. There has never been so much mystery in one of the books prior. Who put Harry's name into the Goblet of Fire? What's Snape's real deal? Can Dumbledore be any more freaking awesome!? 
 This book turns the whole series on its head. In the first three books, Voldemort is nothing more than an insubstantial idea that the whole wizarding world is afraid of. Now he's back and ready to wreak some more havoc. Goblet of Fire is the turning point in both the series and Harry's life as a young wizard. From here on out he knows (even though he doesn't truly learn his destiny just yet) that the only reason he's alive is to stop Voldemort. While it's not really discussed, once Harry sees Voldemort rise again, he takes it as a personal challenge to avenge his parents and all the lives that were destroyed during Voldemort's previous reign of terror. 
 In my personal opinion, this is the best book in the series for all those reason. Even after reading it for the ninth time, I still love flying through the Triwizard Tournament with Harry and still get choked up when Dumbledore salutes Cedric Diggory at the end. F**cking epic!

Wow I teared up in some unusual spots this time. Every time Molly got all "protective mother" over Harry it really got to me. Also when Molly and Bill showed up to watch Harry for the last task, and Harry was so suprised and happy, I just had to stop reading and really think about what the Weasleys mean to him, how they really are the family he never got to have. It made me so emotional, and I wonder whether it's because as I grow older I can appreciate the importance of family (however dysfunctional) more or see it better from Molly's perspective and understand the love she has for him. 
 Cedrics story also really got to me a lot this read around. Maybe because of the affinity I've gained towards Hufflepuff since the last time read it. I have a feeling that I've also just possibly forgotten how all the details of the book really do make you feel. There were a few points of detail surrounding the death eaters that hit me like I was reading them for the first time. And whether I'd forgotten them or because of my more mature perspective they felt really brutal. Either way Harry Potter never fails to teach me something new no matter how many times I reread it. Once you start getting into these later books they really have strong core messages while the stories just get more complex and my love for them is unending.

 Two days later, I'd finished the re-read.

I love, love, love the fourth book in the Harry Potter series. I started reading this series only because my son was gaga over it and BEGGED me to read it. Lord knows I've watched the movies at least one hundred times with him - and I'm NOT exaggerating. So I was delighted when I could not put this book down and looked forward to reading it every evening after work and on the weekends. If I'm given the choice of which movie to watch out of the series, I inevitably chose #4 or #7 as they are by far my favorites.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Dumbledore really shines in this book. We are shown a very different side of him and it is written incredibly well. The return of Voldemort was spectacular, the death of Cedric tragic, and the moment that "Mad-Eye" was revealed to be the culprit literally made me stand up and scream in disbelief. This is a masterfully woven story. I'm still dying to know what Snape's true purpose in the story is. I don't know why, but he is one of my favorite characters. My son knows, and I've threatened to ground him for life if he spoils it for me!

book_b.title: Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (Harry Potter, #2)

sample_reviews.review_text: I have no idea why everyone maligns this book as the worst of the series. It's way more interesting than the first book, with a much more thrilling mystery and better characterization. Pretty much the only thing wrong with it is its not as good as the five books that follow it.

I read this one aloud to the kids. It's fun to go back and read Harry Potter with fresh eyes. This one always seemed like one of the weaker stories in the bunch, which is odd because it's so foundational for what comes later. In some ways it's surprising how much the adults let things slide--it's full of racist undertones (mudbloods) that are never squashed and Dumbledore does basically nothing to stop an attack on the school. It's a good thing Harry figured it all out. Between this and his hiring of Lockhardt, you start to wonder if Dumbledore has completely lost it.

Currently re-reading the one and only Harry Potter. I forgot how much more light-hearted the first few were which is saying something considering this book contains murder, dangerous beasts and the possessing spirit of a dark lord.

AUDIO-REVIEW 
 I am just slowly working my way through all the Harry Potter audio books and I have to say, they are so much fun. As someone who has only ever seen the movies, and couldn't get into the paperbacks, the audio-books are captivating. It's fascinating to see the differences between the movie and the books. I wonder if at the time, fans were upset with them or if people just accepted it. 
 It's not my favorite Harry Potter book but it lays a great deal of foundation and now that I know the entire Harry Potter story, I find myself listening and trying to detect hints of foreshadowing, indicators of the future. It makes listening to the audio-books so much more enjoyable. I also learned that Gilderoy Lockhart might be one of the most conceded, self-centered characters I have ever come across in reading. He really is just atrocious, but none the less it is fun to watch Harry mature and enjoy another year of Hogwart adventures!

Fun book to read with my 8-year-old son. Lots of mystery and making connections. 
 Recommended.

 Goblet of Fire is where things start to get truly awesome. The first three books in the series follow a pretty rigid formula: pre-Hogwarts -> at Hogwarts -> Malfoy is annoy/classes are almost a sidenote -> harry & co find out something sinister is going on -> investigation while dealing with quidditch worries -> reveal -> Harry stops Voldemort from coming back -> everyone smiles. Goblet of Fire, while loosely following that same formula, breaks free of the restrictions and does something different. Quidditch is replaced with the Triwizard tournament and sh!t is just straight cray-cray for Harry. There has never been so much mystery in one of the books prior. Who put Harry's name into the Goblet of Fire? What's Snape's real deal? Can Dumbledore be any more freaking awesome!? 
 This book turns the whole series on its head. In the first three books, Voldemort is nothing more than an insubstantial idea that the whole wizarding world is afraid of. Now he's back and ready to wreak some more havoc. Goblet of Fire is the turning point in both the series and Harry's life as a young wizard. From here on out he knows (even though he doesn't truly learn his destiny just yet) that the only reason he's alive is to stop Voldemort. While it's not really discussed, once Harry sees Voldemort rise again, he takes it as a personal challenge to avenge his parents and all the lives that were destroyed during Voldemort's previous reign of terror.
