For many, these series of books are considered to be a Harry Potter rip-off but in reality they are just following the established formula of all teen/children adventures. So it is a fine book at what it's all about but hardly feels special if you have read or watched enough of the same type. 
 So, as the stereotype dictates, the hero is a boy who is treated at first as a looser before he is revealed to be the son of a God and taken to train to a special school of half-breeds just like him. Throw in some basic Greek mythology, lots of monsters, some conspiracy that can destroy the world, and there you go, you get the much familiar path Harry Potter made famous but otherwise did not establish. 
 Just like most such stories, it suffers from what I call "weakened enemies". Since he is constantly fighting monsters and rivals gods, you would expect for him to be some epic-level fighter who does all sorts of stuff but all you see is an everyday boy who can hardly manage at school. It makes all the challenges he faces to pass as pathetic if any kid can beat up a Minotaur with a few sword swings or a Hydra with a hax Medusa head. I am pretty sure most of the target audience won't notice or even care about that, as it feels very cool if a nobody can do all those cool stuff. Yeah, I wonder how many of them realize that this nobody is a demigod who is constantly aided by all sorts of people and other gods just because he was born special. 
 The second thing it suffers from is how the plot seems to drive him and not him driving the plot as it would normally be the case. He is just running from one mission to another without really deciding anything for himself, or even accomplishing anything with his own strength or cunningness. Heck, even I could rival the gods if had for free all the allies and equipment he gets. Just think of all the main events he was part of. 
 - Fending off the Fury because someone intervened. 
 - Accused of being a thief without having a saying in the whole thing. 
 - Fending off the Minotaur because of a magic sword someone else gave him. 
 - Taken to the training camp without choosing it. 
 - Finding a way to save his mother through someone else, whom he didn't even ask for help. 
 - Beating the Medusa with a pitiful excuse. 
 - Beating Hades without really fighting him. He was betrayed. 
 - Fighting the real villain with the powers his father gave him. 
 So he feels too much like a plot device instead of a boy who tries to fight his destiny or something like that. He never even questions his own status but rather runs after the more experienced ones. 
 The third problem is the villain of the book, rather easy to tell who it's going to be despite being hidden. The main conflict of the book also makes no sense at all. If the lightning bolt was so powerful and precious, how was it stolen so easily by a nobody? How can anyone blame Percy as the thief when he never went to the temple of the gods or didn't even know they exist? If the villain knew how to go to the underworld, why didn't he just go there himself? And what a classic, when revealed he just explains his plan in detail, as if it matters at all to someone he plans on killing a few minutes later. 
 The fourth problem is quite minor if you are not Greek. I am and I found all this bastardization of my country's mythology rather insulting. All of a sudden the whole realm of the gods is at some American soil and the three main gods are rivals. Oh come on! 
 But I guess it is a fine line of books for kids since the plot is rather fast and it has magic and monsters and gods and stuff happening every few pages. Cool but hardly great.

This series appealed to me when the movie was in the theater but I was busy and never got to it. When I saw that it was soon being released on DVD I decided I wanted to read the book before seeing the movie. I belong to the school of though that most of the time, the book is better than the movie and this is another story that I believe that holds true for. 
 I shared this book with my children, we read almost the entire thing aloud and then borrowed the audio book to listen to in the car on a long trip. One thing I liked about listening was hearing someone else pronounce the names for the Greek gods, I just wasn't entirely sure of the pronunciation of some of them which is no big deal when you are reading silently to yourself but becomes a bigger problem when you are reading aloud! 
 Parts of this book reminded me of Harry Potter (another series I am working through with my children this summer) and somewhat of the Spiderwick Chronicles which we have already finished. I like that this opened their minds to the idea of Greek myths because I think we are going to moving into those in a few weeks. This book was engrossing enough for adults or children and I highly recommend it. When we went to the beach last week my children were throwing shells back in telling me that they were offering for Poseidon the sea god!

I don't know if it was all the hoopla I've heard about this that built it up too much in my head, or what. I closed the book with a shrug of the shoulders and a "meh" on my lips, feeling resoundingly underwhelmed. i started reading it to my somewhat timid 9 yo son. He was too scared of the monsters and asked me to pick a different book to read to him. I had to finish it on my own. The only plus I can see from reading it is that I now have a better grasp of who some of the Greek gods are. So there's something at least! I'm still undecided if I will finish the series or not.

sample_reviews.review_text:
OMG. I'm once again dumped head first into the world of Harry Potter. 
 I absolutely love how JK Rowling feeds us a bit of information and it turns out to be useful in the end. Nothing goes to waste and nothing is without purpose. GoF is more action based than it's precedents and things really go up a notch. Now, we really see the reality of being Harry Potter hit him. Before this, while it isn't always nice, it's a lot of fanfare and roses. I saw this thing on Tumble saying how in books 1-3, Harry is all like 'Fuck yeah! I'm Harry Potter!' and in books 4-6, he's like 'Fuck, I'm Harry Potter.' HHahahhaa that's really accurate.
Reread December 2016. Still as exciting and heartbreaking and incredible as ever.

I know a lot of people that think this book is one of the worst of the series. Worst being a loosely used term considering it's Harry Potter. Kind of like how Temple of Doom is considered the worst Indiana Jones movie, but it's still awesome because it's Indiana Jones. Anyway, those people are insane in the membrane. 
 Goblet of Fire is where things start to get truly awesome. The first three books in the series follow a pretty rigid formula: pre-Hogwarts -> at Hogwarts -> Malfoy is annoy/classes are almost a sidenote -> harry & co find out something sinister is going on -> investigation while dealing with quidditch worries -> reveal -> Harry stops Voldemort from coming back -> everyone smiles. Goblet of Fire, while loosely following that same formula, breaks free of the restrictions and does something different. Quidditch is replaced with the Triwizard tournament and sh!t is just straight cray-cray for Harry. There has never been so much mystery in one of the books prior. Who put Harry's name into the Goblet of Fire? What's Snape's real deal? Can Dumbledore be any more freaking awesome!? 
 This book turns the whole series on its head. In the first three books, Voldemort is nothing more than an insubstantial idea that the whole wizarding world is afraid of. Now he's back and ready to wreak some more havoc. Goblet of Fire is the turning point in both the series and Harry's life as a young wizard. From here on out he knows (even though he doesn't truly learn his destiny just yet) that the only reason he's alive is to stop Voldemort. While it's not really discussed, once Harry sees Voldemort rise again, he takes it as a personal challenge to avenge his parents and all the lives that were destroyed during Voldemort's previous reign of terror. 
 In my personal opinion, this is the best book in the series for all those reason. Even after reading it for the ninth time, I still love flying through the Triwizard Tournament with Harry and still get choked up when Dumbledore salutes Cedric Diggory at the end. F**cking epic!

book_a.title: The Battle of the Labyrinth (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #4)

sample_reviews.review_text:
The Battle Of The Labyrinth (Percy Jackson And The Olympians #4), by Rick Riordan 
 Synopsis: Percy Jackson isn't expecting freshman orientation to be any fun. But when a mysterious mortal acquaintance appears on campus, followed by demon cheerleaders, things quickly move from bad to worse. 
 In this fourth installment of the blockbuster series, time is running out as war between the Olympians and the evil Titan lord Kronos draws near. Even the safe haven of Camp Half-Blood grows more vulnerable by the minute as Kronos's army prepares to invade its once impenetrable borders. To stop the invasion, Percy and his demigod friends must set out on a quest through the Labyrinth - a sprawling underground world with stunning surprises at every turn. 
 In A Sentence: A decent read, but I'm not feeling very wowed by this series (not yet anyway) 
 My Thoughts: At this point I admit I'm starting to just power through the series. It's a fun series that kids and young adults would really enjoy, but as an adult I don't feel as wowed as I could be. The chapter titles still pull a chuckle out of me, and there are sentences peppered throughout the story that are also pretty funny (case in point: "You hit the Lord of the Titans in the eye with a blue plastic hairbrush"). Ridiculous scenarios seem to be the main trademark of these books, which is always fun, but beyond that, the story doesn't hold a whole lot of depth. It's your typical action novels: lots of energy and a fast-paced plot, but very little depth and complexity. 
 Would I recommend this read? Of course! It's easy-going fun that doesn't require too much concentration. It's ridiculously funny in parts, and the incorporation of Greek Mythology into today's world is loads of fun to read about. Plus, it's a fast read, perfect for your next vacation. I'm starting the final book now and I'm looking forward to seeing how it ends. Happy reading!

This series keeps getting better and better. When I was a kid I had always liked the stories of Icarus and Dadeulus. This series is enjoyable and engaging now, if I had read them as a kid I would have been obsessed with them.

I'm not sure what I said for the Titan's Curse by Rick Riordan, but honestly, this book is my fave so far. I can't even remember what happened in the Titan's Curse because I was just sooo intrigued by this storyline. A job well done!
This series actually groves on me. It is pretty good

Still really enjoying this series. I find it interesting that, as Percy and his friends grow up, the gods are shown less as the all-powerful 15 foot high beings of the earlier books, and instead as rather more 'human' figures. Big fat metaphor for teenagers learning to relate to the adults in their lives, perhaps? I know that even though neither made long appearances, I loved both Poseidon and Dionysus in this book. 
 So many legends were woven into this book that I'm now feeling slightly dizzy - not that that's a bad thing. I like that the stories are growing more complicated. Also, having read books 2, 3 & 4 within a few days, I don't have clear delineations between them in my own mind - entirely my own fault! I think I'll take a short break before reading the final book - but not a very long one, because I'm looking forward to finding out how the overall story ends. 
 Read for the Seasonal Reading Challenge Winter 09/10 task 10.4 (Winner's Choice: Kari )

I've seen the movies and loved them so I thought it was about time I saw where everything began for Percy, Grover and Annabeth. The Lightning Thief by Rick Riordan tells the story of how twelve year old Percy Jackson discovers he's a demigod. Son of Poseidon, Percy has never quite been like other kids. Hidden in the mortal world to protect him from those with grudges against his biological father, Percy has always known that he was different. When Zeus' lightning bolt is stolen, Percy's existence comes to light and his paternity is revealed. If Percy is to find the bolt (and consequentially save his mother and become a hero) - he needs to overcome monsters and battle gods. Not alone in his quest, his best friend Grover and one of Athena's daughters, Annabeth, tag along to give Percy the best chance against the powerful immortals. 
 For the right audience, I believe this book would be perfect. There's action and adventure. A great take on classic mythology and characters I could fall in love with. 
 The problem is - I'm not the right audience. I'm in my twenties and unlike a lot of other young adult and middle grade books I've read - this one made me feel old in a way no other book I've read before has. 
 The characters, as entertaining as they are, read a little young. I liked that they are true to their character. I believe that Percy is twelve despite him having to try and take on challenges that would terrify people many times his age. And the author is consistent with the the trio's skill levels. I just think that I'm not the right person for this book. The mythology is amazing. I love how much Riordan packed in. There's all sorts of gods met and mentioned with places and stories being inserted into the plot all over the place. Journey wise - it didn't feel very planned all the time. Like the trio were sort of stumbling upon where they were supposed to go next. But in the end they got to where they were meant to be so it all worked out for the best I suppose. 
 I'll still watch the movies (provided they make more! Fingers crossed!) but this series isn't for me.
I liked it but I wasn't so into it like Harry Potter. I think boys would really enjoy it and it's not as scary or dark as Harry Potter.

Even now, I am still reading Rick Riordan books. I just can't get enough. The characters he wrote were ( and still are ) memorable and full of heart, and that's hard to write off.

 And also.. All the chapter names were a summary of the chapter. Why... Why... Chapter 123 would have worked for me. 
 All the missions Percy went on reminded me very much of a video game.. Every step of the way there was some pathetic obstacle, he pressed "up, down, up, up, triangle, square, circle, up, r2" and it was over. So predictable and so meh.. 
 I'm reading the second one because im determined to get through.. I have hopes it will improve.

I've seen the movies and loved them so I thought it was about time I saw where everything began for Percy, Grover and Annabeth. The Lightning Thief by Rick Riordan tells the story of how twelve year old Percy Jackson discovers he's a demigod. Son of Poseidon, Percy has never quite been like other kids. Hidden in the mortal world to protect him from those with grudges against his biological father, Percy has always known that he was different. When Zeus' lightning bolt is stolen, Percy's existence comes to light and his paternity is revealed. If Percy is to find the bolt (and consequentially save his mother and become a hero) - he needs to overcome monsters and battle gods. Not alone in his quest, his best friend Grover and one of Athena's daughters, Annabeth, tag along to give Percy the best chance against the powerful immortals. 
 For the right audience, I believe this book would be perfect. There's action and adventure. A great take on classic mythology and characters I could fall in love with. 
 The problem is - I'm not the right audience. I'm in my twenties and unlike a lot of other young adult and middle grade books I've read - this one made me feel old in a way no other book I've read before has. 
 The characters, as entertaining as they are, read a little young. I liked that they are true to their character. I believe that Percy is twelve despite him having to try and take on challenges that would terrify people many times his age. And the author is consistent with the the trio's skill levels. I just think that I'm not the right person for this book. The mythology is amazing. I love how much Riordan packed in. There's all sorts of gods met and mentioned with places and stories being inserted into the plot all over the place. Journey wise - it didn't feel very planned all the time. Like the trio were sort of stumbling upon where they were supposed to go next. But in the end they got to where they were meant to be so it all worked out for the best I suppose. 
 I'll still watch the movies (provided they make more! Fingers crossed!) but this series isn't for me.
I liked it but I wasn't so into it like Harry Potter. I think boys would really enjoy it and it's not as scary or dark as Harry Potter.

The Percy Jackson series was the first major series I had read; and I was obsessed from the very first word. Needless to say, I'm a big fan of the series. From the hilarious narration from Percy, to the wonderful combination of the modern world and Greek myths, this series was a recipe for goodness from the start. Even now, I am still reading Rick Riordan books. I just can't get enough. The characters he wrote were ( and still are ) memorable and full of heart, and that's hard to write off.
couldn't finish it

For many, these series of books are considered to be a Harry Potter rip-off but in reality they are just following the established formula of all teen/children adventures. So it is a fine book at what it's all about but hardly feels special if you have read or watched enough of the same type. 
 So, as the stereotype dictates, the hero is a boy who is treated at first as a looser before he is revealed to be the son of a God and taken to train to a special school of half-breeds just like him. Throw in some basic Greek mythology, lots of monsters, some conspiracy that can destroy the world, and there you go, you get the much familiar path Harry Potter made famous but otherwise did not establish. 
 Just like most such stories, it suffers from what I call "weakened enemies". Since he is constantly fighting monsters and rivals gods, you would expect for him to be some epic-level fighter who does all sorts of stuff but all you see is an everyday boy who can hardly manage at school. It makes all the challenges he faces to pass as pathetic if any kid can beat up a Minotaur with a few sword swings or a Hydra with a hax Medusa head. I am pretty sure most of the target audience won't notice or even care about that, as it feels very cool if a nobody can do all those cool stuff. Yeah, I wonder how many of them realize that this nobody is a demigod who is constantly aided by all sorts of people and other gods just because he was born special. 
 The second thing it suffers from is how the plot seems to drive him and not him driving the plot as it would normally be the case. He is just running from one mission to another without really deciding anything for himself, or even accomplishing anything with his own strength or cunningness. Heck, even I could rival the gods if had for free all the allies and equipment he gets. Just think of all the main events he was part of. 
 - Fending off the Fury because someone intervened. 
 - Accused of being a thief without having a saying in the whole thing. 
 - Fending off the Minotaur because of a magic sword someone else gave him. 
 - Taken to the training camp without choosing it. 
 - Finding a way to save his mother through someone else, whom he didn't even ask for help. 
 - Beating the Medusa with a pitiful excuse. 
 - Beating Hades without really fighting him. He was betrayed. 
 - Fighting the real villain with the powers his father gave him. 
 So he feels too much like a plot device instead of a boy who tries to fight his destiny or something like that. He never even questions his own status but rather runs after the more experienced ones. 
 The third problem is the villain of the book, rather easy to tell who it's going to be despite being hidden. The main conflict of the book also makes no sense at all. If the lightning bolt was so powerful and precious, how was it stolen so easily by a nobody? How can anyone blame Percy as the thief when he never went to the temple of the gods or didn't even know they exist? If the villain knew how to go to the underworld, why didn't he just go there himself? And what a classic, when revealed he just explains his plan in detail, as if it matters at all to someone he plans on killing a few minutes later. 
 The fourth problem is quite minor if you are not Greek. I am and I found all this bastardization of my country's mythology rather insulting. All of a sudden the whole realm of the gods is at some American soil and the three main gods are rivals. Oh come on! 
 But I guess it is a fine line of books for kids since the plot is rather fast and it has magic and monsters and gods and stuff happening every few pages. Cool but hardly great.

This series appealed to me when the movie was in the theater but I was busy and never got to it. When I saw that it was soon being released on DVD I decided I wanted to read the book before seeing the movie. I belong to the school of though that most of the time, the book is better than the movie and this is another story that I believe that holds true for. 
 I shared this book with my children, we read almost the entire thing aloud and then borrowed the audio book to listen to in the car on a long trip. One thing I liked about listening was hearing someone else pronounce the names for the Greek gods, I just wasn't entirely sure of the pronunciation of some of them which is no big deal when you are reading silently to yourself but becomes a bigger problem when you are reading aloud! 
 Parts of this book reminded me of Harry Potter (another series I am working through with my children this summer) and somewhat of the Spiderwick Chronicles which we have already finished. I like that this opened their minds to the idea of Greek myths because I think we are going to moving into those in a few weeks. This book was engrossing enough for adults or children and I highly recommend it. When we went to the beach last week my children were throwing shells back in telling me that they were offering for Poseidon the sea god!

I don't know if it was all the hoopla I've heard about this that built it up too much in my head, or what. I closed the book with a shrug of the shoulders and a "meh" on my lips, feeling resoundingly underwhelmed. i started reading it to my somewhat timid 9 yo son. He was too scared of the monsters and asked me to pick a different book to read to him. I had to finish it on my own. The only plus I can see from reading it is that I now have a better grasp of who some of the Greek gods are. So there's something at least! I'm still undecided if I will finish the series or not.

book_b.title: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (Harry Potter, #4)

sample_reviews.review_text:
OMG. I'm once again dumped head first into the world of Harry Potter. 
 I absolutely love how JK Rowling feeds us a bit of information and it turns out to be useful in the end. Nothing goes to waste and nothing is without purpose. GoF is more action based than it's precedents and things really go up a notch. Now, we really see the reality of being Harry Potter hit him. Before this, while it isn't always nice, it's a lot of fanfare and roses. I saw this thing on Tumble saying how in books 1-3, Harry is all like 'Fuck yeah! I'm Harry Potter!' and in books 4-6, he's like 'Fuck, I'm Harry Potter.' HHahahhaa that's really accurate.
Reread December 2016. Still as exciting and heartbreaking and incredible as ever.

I know a lot of people that think this book is one of the worst of the series. Worst being a loosely used term considering it's Harry Potter. Kind of like how Temple of Doom is considered the worst Indiana Jones movie, but it's still awesome because it's Indiana Jones. Anyway, those people are insane in the membrane. 
 Goblet of Fire is where things start to get truly awesome. The first three books in the series follow a pretty rigid formula: pre-Hogwarts -> at Hogwarts -> Malfoy is annoy/classes are almost a sidenote -> harry & co find out something sinister is going on -> investigation while dealing with quidditch worries -> reveal -> Harry stops Voldemort from coming back -> everyone smiles. Goblet of Fire, while loosely following that same formula, breaks free of the restrictions and does something different. Quidditch is replaced with the Triwizard tournament and sh!t is just straight cray-cray for Harry. There has never been so much mystery in one of the books prior. Who put Harry's name into the Goblet of Fire? What's Snape's real deal? Can Dumbledore be any more freaking awesome!? 
 This book turns the whole series on its head. In the first three books, Voldemort is nothing more than an insubstantial idea that the whole wizarding world is afraid of. Now he's back and ready to wreak some more havoc. Goblet of Fire is the turning point in both the series and Harry's life as a young wizard. From here on out he knows (even though he doesn't truly learn his destiny just yet) that the only reason he's alive is to stop Voldemort. While it's not really discussed, once Harry sees Voldemort rise again, he takes it as a personal challenge to avenge his parents and all the lives that were destroyed during Voldemort's previous reign of terror. 
 In my personal opinion, this is the best book in the series for all those reason. Even after reading it for the ninth time, I still love flying through the Triwizard Tournament with Harry and still get choked up when Dumbledore salutes Cedric Diggory at the end. F**cking epic!

** spoiler alert ** 
 Book 4 was definately a great one. It's the first time you get the sense that the characters are really starting to grow up. With the dance, and the Tri-Wizard competition and all. It also felt a lot more adult becuase it's the first book in the series where someone actually dies.
Emiri: 2007

This is the 4th book in the HP series and marks the turning point in the series, where it becomes darker and more dangerous for Harry and friends. Mixed in with all of that, the plot centers around the Tri-Wizard Tournament, a notoriously dangerous competition between the top three wizarding schools. This book introduces numerous colorful and well-developed characters, and gives us an idea of the wizarding world outside our beloved Hogwart's.
Mi libro favorito de Harry Potter hasta ahora... Y debo agregar que tambien mi pelicula! Ojala siga siendo asi cuando lea los otros 3 libros!
Absolutely loved this book and I have to say, probably my favorite of the series so far. Mysterious, exhilarating, and overall just extraordinary - this book will keep you wanting more!

Incredible. J.K. Rowling is a master storyteller, I was shocked,scared,sad,happy,angry throughout this whole book. Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire begins the darker side of the Harry Potter books. It is the transitioning book out of middlegrade/children's books and into a older more adult series. It slowed down for me in the middle of the book between the Quidditch World Cup and the actual begining of the Triwizard Tournament but it picked back up the pace and the last 200 pages will keep you on the edge of your seat. This was the first Harry Potter book that made me cry but I know that it won't be the last. Amazing if you haven't read this series yet go get the books and read them they are more than worth it.

My absolute favorite of the Harry Potter books (the finale as its only equal), I loved this book... seriously, I don't even know what to say! It was so amazing it knocked the wind right out of me and I'm speechless. Really, I'm sitting here with a dazed look on my face right now!

 I shared this book with my children, we read almost the entire thing aloud and then borrowed the audio book to listen to in the car on a long trip. One thing I liked about listening was hearing someone else pronounce the names for the Greek gods, I just wasn't entirely sure of the pronunciation of some of them which is no big deal when you are reading silently to yourself but becomes a bigger problem when you are reading aloud! 
 Parts of this book reminded me of Harry Potter (another series I am working through with my children this summer) and somewhat of the Spiderwick Chronicles which we have already finished. I like that this opened their minds to the idea of Greek myths because I think we are going to moving into those in a few weeks. This book was engrossing enough for adults or children and I highly recommend it. When we went to the beach last week my children were throwing shells back in telling me that they were offering for Poseidon the sea god!

I don't know if it was all the hoopla I've heard about this that built it up too much in my head, or what. I closed the book with a shrug of the shoulders and a "meh" on my lips, feeling resoundingly underwhelmed. i started reading it to my somewhat timid 9 yo son. He was too scared of the monsters and asked me to pick a different book to read to him. I had to finish it on my own. The only plus I can see from reading it is that I now have a better grasp of who some of the Greek gods are. So there's something at least! I'm still undecided if I will finish the series or not.

I'm Harry Potter!' and in books 4-6, he's like 'Fuck, I'm Harry Potter.' HHahahhaa that's really accurate.
Reread December 2016. Still as exciting and heartbreaking and incredible as ever.

I know a lot of people that think this book is one of the worst of the series. Worst being a loosely used term considering it's Harry Potter. Kind of like how Temple of Doom is considered the worst Indiana Jones movie, but it's still awesome because it's Indiana Jones. Anyway, those people are insane in the membrane. 
 Goblet of Fire is where things start to get truly awesome. The first three books in the series follow a pretty rigid formula: pre-Hogwarts -> at Hogwarts -> Malfoy is annoy/classes are almost a sidenote -> harry & co find out something sinister is going on -> investigation while dealing with quidditch worries -> reveal -> Harry stops Voldemort from coming back -> everyone smiles. Goblet of Fire, while loosely following that same formula, breaks free of the restrictions and does something different. Quidditch is replaced with the Triwizard tournament and sh!t is just straight cray-cray for Harry. There has never been so much mystery in one of the books prior. Who put Harry's name into the Goblet of Fire? What's Snape's real deal? Can Dumbledore be any more freaking awesome!? 
 This book turns the whole series on its head. In the first three books, Voldemort is nothing more than an insubstantial idea that the whole wizarding world is afraid of. Now he's back and ready to wreak some more havoc. Goblet of Fire is the turning point in both the series and Harry's life as a young wizard. From here on out he knows (even though he doesn't truly learn his destiny just yet) that the only reason he's alive is to stop Voldemort. While it's not really discussed, once Harry sees Voldemort rise again, he takes it as a personal challenge to avenge his parents and all the lives that were destroyed during Voldemort's previous reign of terror. 
 In my personal opinion, this is the best book in the series for all those reason. Even after reading it for the ninth time, I still love flying through the Triwizard Tournament with Harry and still get choked up when Dumbledore salutes Cedric Diggory at the end. F**cking epic!

reference_book.title: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (Harry Potter, #4)
reference_book.review_text:
Like I mentioned before, this series splits (for me) into the first three books on one side, and the last books on the other. This review pertains to the last books in the series. 
 After reading the first books in the series, I was a bit disheartened, but was encouraged by a lot of people to give the last few books a try. And after reading them, I have to say, they're a huge improvement and much more entertaining. It's like the series "grew up." The last few books have a much better plot and character development. Less cheesy dialogue is also nice. These books are an easy and addictive read. 
 I will say one thing, though. The most annoying thing about these books is that they don't allow the reader to figure anything out on her own. It's like the author is constantly hitting you over the head with the obvious ("Hey! Hey reader! I just made mentioned a detail that I only briefly alluded to a few chapters ago! Did you catch that? You remember that little reference I made, foreshadowing this exact moment?? See! Here it is again! And just in case you don't remember, I will repeat it for you!") For someone who loves puzzles and loves picking up on subtle threads running through the story, I felt a little talked down to. But, if you take the books for what they are, they're very enjoyable.

The book with the greatest potential and the greatest let down. 
 Don't get me wrong, the Harry Potter series (the first four at least) can be enchanting, engaging and a truly worthy read... 
 ... BUT it's not worth the hype. I could name HUNDREDS of books and a score of series that would be a better use of your time than HP but, sadly, did not receive the "hype" this series did. Until the last two, somewhat three, books were read, I was somewhat of a Potter nut. I gave the fourth book five stars for a reason, after all. But starting at the fifth book, the story begins to fall off track. 
 The sixth book was downright disappointing, the fact that a FAN GIRL gets the hero annoyed me, the seventh book, had it's moments, I admit but Rowling should be shot for that pathetic epilogue. I've seen better writing from ten year olds and I am not exaggerating. 
 Over all, I would tell you to try the series out. It's been a great gate-way book into other (more worthy) fantasy books for many, many people and HAS convinced many kids out there that reading can be fun! It's one of the few series out there that I believe will have some historical value because of that fact. 
 If you are looking for an astoundingly great read, however... 
 ... look elsewhere.(

Great book that really will appeal to all ages, not just the target audience of a middle grade reader.

 Harry Potter is orphaned as a baby and send to live with his terrible uncle and aunt, the Dursleys. His cousin, Dudley, is the same age as Harry, and bullies him. Harry's bedroom is the tiny room under the stairs, meanwhile, Dudley has two bedrooms, one to sleep in and one for all of his toys! This is the life that Harry has lived for the past ten years. Then one day a letter arrives for him, but instead of being allowed to read it, his uncle keeps them from Harry. But there is no escape. A giant, named Hagrid shows up and explains to Harry what his aunt and uncle have been hiding; Harry is a wizard! 
 Next thing Harry knows he is off to a special school where he finally makes friends. He also has some enemies, but for the first time in his life, he feels like he belongs. I love the way this book is written. There is humor and creativity. Harry finds himself in one adventure after another, and he also learns what it is like to have people care for you. Great book that really will appeal to all ages, not just the target audience of a middle grade reader.

sample_reviews.review_text:
OMG. I'm once again dumped head first into the world of Harry Potter. 
 I absolutely love how JK Rowling feeds us a bit of information and it turns out to be useful in the end. Nothing goes to waste and nothing is without purpose. GoF is more action based than it's precedents and things really go up a notch. Now, we really see the reality of being Harry Potter hit him. Before this, while it isn't always nice, it's a lot of fanfare and roses. I saw this thing on Tumble saying how in books 1-3, Harry is all like 'Fuck yeah! I'm Harry Potter!' and in books 4-6, he's like 'Fuck, I'm Harry Potter.' HHahahhaa that's really accurate.

Goblet of Fire is the bestest of best Harry Potter novels. It's bold, full of unexpected twists and turns and the usual Rowling formula- wit and humor, plot that is beyond magic, characters that breathe, the amalgamation of darkness and light, the subjects I wished I enrolled, the magical creatures I wished I've seen before and now. 
 You can't just put it down and it turned out that I was lost in time that I finished reading it 1:30 in the morning, when I thought it was just the setting of the sun. Goblet of Fire is romancing the readers, but not making them fools. You just can't dictate how the story should be because Rowling's version will always be the bestest of best. 
 The rise of the Dark Arts and Wizards turned out to be one of the outstanding addition to a foolproof plot. 
 When I've finished reading it, I can't coerce myself to sleep because I want to know what's next and you want to relieve the moments you just have read, as if you were a part of it. 
 I promised myself to reread it, even if it means to do it 77 times 7.

I know a lot of people that think this book is one of the worst of the series. Worst being a loosely used term considering it's Harry Potter. Kind of like how Temple of Doom is considered the worst Indiana Jones movie, but it's still awesome because it's Indiana Jones. Anyway, those people are insane in the membrane. 
 Goblet of Fire is where things start to get truly awesome. The first three books in the series follow a pretty rigid formula: pre-Hogwarts -> at Hogwarts -> Malfoy is annoy/classes are almost a sidenote -> harry & co find out something sinister is going on -> investigation while dealing with quidditch worries -> reveal -> Harry stops Voldemort from coming back -> everyone smiles. Goblet of Fire, while loosely following that same formula, breaks free of the restrictions and does something different. Quidditch is replaced with the Triwizard tournament and sh!t is just straight cray-cray for Harry. There has never been so much mystery in one of the books prior. Who put Harry's name into the Goblet of Fire? What's Snape's real deal? Can Dumbledore be any more freaking awesome!? 
 This book turns the whole series on its head. In the first three books, Voldemort is nothing more than an insubstantial idea that the whole wizarding world is afraid of. Now he's back and ready to wreak some more havoc. Goblet of Fire is the turning point in both the series and Harry's life as a young wizard. From here on out he knows (even though he doesn't truly learn his destiny just yet) that the only reason he's alive is to stop Voldemort. While it's not really discussed, once Harry sees Voldemort rise again, he takes it as a personal challenge to avenge his parents and all the lives that were destroyed during Voldemort's previous reign of terror. 
 In my personal opinion, this is the best book in the series for all those reason. Even after reading it for the ninth time, I still love flying through the Triwizard Tournament with Harry and still get choked up when Dumbledore salutes Cedric Diggory at the end. F**cking epic!

reference_book.title: Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire (Harry Potter, #4)
reference_book.review_text:
Like I mentioned before, this series splits (for me) into the first three books on one side, and the last books on the other. This review pertains to the last books in the series. 
 After reading the first books in the series, I was a bit disheartened, but was encouraged by a lot of people to give the last few books a try. And after reading them, I have to say, they're a huge improvement and much more entertaining. It's like the series "grew up." The last few books have a much better plot and character development. Less cheesy dialogue is also nice. These books are an easy and addictive read. 
 I will say one thing, though. The most annoying thing about these books is that they don't allow the reader to figure anything out on her own. It's like the author is constantly hitting you over the head with the obvious ("Hey! Hey reader! I just made mentioned a detail that I only briefly alluded to a few chapters ago! Did you catch that? You remember that little reference I made, foreshadowing this exact moment?? See! Here it is again! And just in case you don't remember, I will repeat it for you!") For someone who loves puzzles and loves picking up on subtle threads running through the story, I felt a little talked down to. But, if you take the books for what they are, they're very enjoyable.

 I liked the fact that we get to see Harry as a later-year goer of Hogwarts. He's clearly grown up - from being captain of the Quidditch team to dating Ginny Weasely. This is perhaps the most tightly wound of all the books, that which contains the most plot and both answers and sets up so many questions, resolves and promises almost too much. Wow! Holy crap!!! I just read this book in two days, I couldn't put it down, and that's quite a feat having two small children! This is now my favorite book of the series. Way better than the movie. The book explains so much more about Voldemort's life that I understand him now as a character, his strengths and weaknesses. Character development and relationships are so much better explained in the book rather than the movie. I can't wait to crack open the next book! I've only seen the last movies once so I feel as if I'm going into the last book a little blind. I am so thankful I went ahead and read the books anyway because I understand way more than I ever could have just relying on the movies!
Full discussion here (with spoilers): https://cutloosebookloose.wordpress.c...

The book with the greatest potential and the greatest let down. 
 Don't get me wrong, the Harry Potter series (the first four at least) can be enchanting, engaging and a truly worthy read... 
 ... BUT it's not worth the hype. I could name HUNDREDS of books and a score of series that would be a better use of your time than HP but, sadly, did not receive the "hype" this series did. Until the last two, somewhat three, books were read, I was somewhat of a Potter nut. I gave the fourth book five stars for a reason, after all. But starting at the fifth book, the story begins to fall off track. 
 The sixth book was downright disappointing, the fact that a FAN GIRL gets the hero annoyed me, the seventh book, had it's moments, I admit but Rowling should be shot for that pathetic epilogue. I've seen better writing from ten year olds and I am not exaggerating. 
 Over all, I would tell you to try the series out. It's been a great gate-way book into other (more worthy) fantasy books for many, many people and HAS convinced many kids out there that reading can be fun! It's one of the few series out there that I believe will have some historical value because of that fact. 
 If you are looking for an astoundingly great read, however... 
 ... look elsewhere.(

Malfoy always taunts Harry, Ron, and Hermione. Snape always hates Harry and the Griffyndors for no apparent reason, and his bias is never questioned. Lee Jordan always swears at the Quidditch matches and gets scolded by McGonnogal. Harry always manages to barely catch the snitch just in time to win a Quidditch match for Gryffindor. Harry and Ron always suck at classes while Hermione gets shamed for doing well. 
 See how I revealed no spoilers there? 
 There's only so much of the same thing you can read over and over again before it all blends together into a boring mess. Five books of this?! With the plot drawn out for hundreds of useless pages? Why would I want to endure three ignorant teenagers complaining about not being told anything, while they whisper secrets in the open and lazily sit by watching the action go on around them? Why can't I be in on the big-kids' table, and help the adults put things together? While reading this I constantly had to ask myself... How are these good characters again? There's something wrong when the two-dimensional side characters are more intriguing than your three musketeers. 
 Hmm, I wonder why it's so hard to ignore the school bully long enough, so you can keep playing your favorite sport, Harry? 
 Hmm, it must be hard to control a conversation long enough to say what you want to your own godfather, Harry. 
 Hmm, so you want to "burn" the useful gift your brilliant friend gave you for help, Harry? You and your best friend pay no attention when Hermione, the successful student, tries to help your study schedule (never thought that might help you become an Auror, did you, Harry?). That must have something to do with the fact that you haven't yet realized how reading actually helps in real life, dear Harry. 
 Hmm, I wonder why it's a bad idea your mind is linked with Voldemort's, Harry. 
 Hmm, could it be a good idea to guard your mind from your worst enemy, Harry? 
 Hmm, how about you stop complaining and learn from the people you envy or criticize, Harry? 
 Please tell me why anyone would like reading 600 pages of dull plot surrounding this guy's attitude problems? I don't get it. 
 The only new material in this one is Umbridge's infernal presence, which was entertaining. But Rowling took 800+ pages to retell the same story she's done four times before, inserting maybe 20% new material, while boring me with the rest of the useless rambling junk. Stop killing so many trees and use less of my time. Stop asking so many questions, and make something actually happen. Stop writing about hormonal teenager problems, and give me morality and suspense. Give fewer homework troubles to your idiot main character, and describe more of the legacy behind everything actually driving this plot. Stop feeding me the same patronizing slop... I can see through it. 
 At least the last 200 pages are interesting. 
 Why are all the side characters seemingly more interesting than the protagonist? It's because Rowling refuses to actually use the entire 800 pages for character development. Instead she crams all the good action into the last 5-7 chapters (making me guilty for feeling happy, after struggling through the slothful 600 previous pages). 
 This book earns 3 stars only for Rowling's inventive creations in the wizarding world, and the last 7 chapters which made the whole 800+ pages of drudgery somewhat worth it. But when the environment is more interesting than the plot... Errrrr... There's a problem. 
 I'm sorry, but if you've failed to make your hero interesting by the fifth book, just stop... stop using your international fame to put me through this mediocre excuse for a saga... It was interesting in book one, Rowling, because that one was 200 pages. And maybe you could pass it by me again in book two. But no more... Please no eighth book... Please, I'm begging you... 
 *sigh* Now on to book six: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince. I'm gonna guess that the next 800+ pages have more of the same idiotic lines from Ron that pass for quality children's literature...

3.5 stars [Fantasy] 
 The final showdown at Hogwarts was an impressive muster, but loose ends and deus ex machina keep this from the rating I expected it to earn. 
 The simplistic character interactions that one expects in the first two books continue until the end. We accept teenage irrationality out of our protagonist even, perhaps, as far as The Order of the Phoenix. But the loss of Voldemort's channeled anger, along with the magnitude of extraordinary events that face Harry, makes his puerility of emotion and behavior unrealistic as an of-age savior of the wizarding world. 
 What is the fate of Dolores Umbridge, the insidiously (and unrealistically) evil High Inquisitor? We never hear. How was Draco changed for good? We get a "curt nod" at a train station 19 years later. It is as if an editor told Rowling that she had rambled on too long in Order of the Phoenix and The Half-Blood Prince, so she cut this last book's denouement off at a precipice. Be more concise, don't leave a dozen loose ends! 
 For all the overkill of romance in The Half-Blood Prince, you would think we would get the satisfaction of a celebratory kiss between Harry and Ginny after he never expected to see her again. If I, as a male reader, appreciate this, I imagine that Rowling's female readers are quite disappointed. 
 What kind of magic did the Death Eaters use to overcome a near-invincible magical castle, especially after added protections by the formidable Flitwick? Most jinxes and curses don't hurt fortified stone. Did the defense just sit and allow "reductos" to go off? Did the giants bring engines of war? We are never told. 
 The Deathly Hallows was the most satisfying of Rowling's books, but it ends up quite below the sophistication and excellence of other fantasy. Its popularity may be attributed to base readership and the thrill of the occult, coupled with Rowling's admittedly outstanding character development. The inhumanity of her villains were not credible, her magic system was juvenile, her tactical elements were non-existent, and her sociological axioms and reactions were almost totally divorced from real human animus. 
 This is a pleasing mid-tier fantasy, in spite of its many drawbacks.

reference_book.title: The Titan's Curse (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #3)
reference_book.review_text:
*** "The Titan's Curse" by Rick Riordan, is third in the funny, easy educational series, Percy Jackson & the Olympians. Percy, son of Poseidon, the sea god, follows a half-blood (children of Greek gods) quest to rescue Goddess of the Hunt, Athena. The always present personal secondary mission is to save his friend Annabeth, before winter solstice, a few days hence. 
 He joins when Bianca disappears, as foretold by the grimly funny Oracle in camp. Old pals, satyr Grover and Thalia, daughter of Zeus, former guardian tree, team with maiden Huntress ill-fated Zoe, daughter of Atlas. 
 Ubiquitous prophecies and dreams foretell and fill in missing knowledge, such as how Athena was caught. She took on the weight of the world from Annabeth, who was tricked into the job by her treacherous old pal Luke, who was forced by the Titan god Atlas, which explains the book title. 
 Despite a tragic death scene, I liked this book better, maybe because traps, such as the junkyard, were less traditional than in myths. I did recognize Nereus, the stinky Old Man of the Sea, when he had to be trapped to force answers, and Zoe's sisters, the Hesperides with golden apples. Since the garden guardian dragon has stinky breath, is there a smelly theme? 
 I thought a Sun West train would go all the way to San Francisco, where Annabeth's human father helps, but they get off at a deserted mountain resort and trouble follows. At another tour stop, Hoover Dam, the author adds juvenile humor and geography lessons. I do not know if a reader new to greek myths would enjoy the series more. 3.5 stars [Fantasy] 
 The final showdown at Hogwarts was an impressive muster, but loose ends and deus ex machina keep this from the rating I expected it to earn. 
 The simplistic character interactions that one expects in the first two books continue until the end. We accept teenage irrationality out of our protagonist even, perhaps, as far as The Order of the Phoenix. But the loss of Voldemort's channeled anger, along with the magnitude of extraordinary events that face Harry, makes his puerility of emotion and behavior unrealistic as an of-age savior of the wizarding world. 
 What is the fate of Dolores Umbridge, the insidiously (and unrealistically) evil High Inquisitor? We never hear. How was Draco changed for good? We get a "curt nod" at a train station 19 years later. It is as if an editor told Rowling that she had rambled on too long in Order of the Phoenix and The Half-Blood Prince, so she cut this last book's denouement off at a precipice. Be more concise, don't leave a dozen loose ends! 
 For all the overkill of romance in The Half-Blood Prince, you would think we would get the satisfaction of a celebratory kiss between Harry and Ginny after he never expected to see her again. If I, as a male reader, appreciate this, I imagine that Rowling's female readers are quite disappointed. 
 What kind of magic did the Death Eaters use to overcome a near-invincible magical castle, especially after added protections by the formidable Flitwick? Most jinxes and curses don't hurt fortified stone. Did the defense just sit and allow "reductos" to go off? Did the giants bring engines of war? We are never told. 
 The Deathly Hallows was the most satisfying of Rowling's books, but it ends up quite below the sophistication and excellence of other fantasy. Its popularity may be attributed to base readership and the thrill of the occult, coupled with Rowling's admittedly outstanding character development. The inhumanity of her villains were not credible, her magic system was juvenile, her tactical elements were non-existent, and her sociological axioms and reactions were almost totally divorced from real human animus. 
 This is a pleasing mid-tier fantasy, in spite of its many drawbacks.

book_b.title: The Sea of Monsters (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #2)

sample_reviews.review_text:
It's been a year since Percy Jackson learned that he is a demigod, the son of his human mother and Poseidon, the Greek God of the sea. On his last day of school, Percy hopes to finish the year without any major disasters and head off to Camp Half Blood, a summer camp for demigods. Unfortunately, trouble has a knack for finding Percy, and he has a run-in with some monsters in gym class. Saved by his friend Annabeth and his classmate Tyson, they escape to camp. 
 Camp Half Blood is not how Percy remembers it. The protective magical boundary of camp is collapsing, monsters are invading the borders, and the camp staff has changed. To make things worse, Percy keeps having dreams about his friend Grover, a satyr on a quest, being in danger. It turns out that Grover has created and "empathy link", allowing him to communicate with Percy from a distance. Between Grover, Hermes, and the Gray Sisters, Percy pieces together clues as to how he can save Camp Half Blood, as well as Grover. Percy's latest quest will take him to the Sea of Monsters, the fabled site of creatures such as Charybdis and the Sirens. In this sequel, Percy will take on old foes and new ones, make new friends, and discover more about his father and family. 
 One of the things I love most about this series is how covertly educational it is! Percy interacts with many characters from Greek mythology and Percy often recalls a quick line or two about the story behind those characters. I recall learning about mythology in grade school and it's fun to revisit those tales. Mention is also given to the works of Greek historians, and I must give kudos to Riordan for making Homer's Odyssey seem interesting! 
 I love how you never know what's going to happen next in this series. Yes, you know something isn't going to be as easy as it initially seems, but you never know who or what to expect! Riordan has a tendency of leading the reader to feel like the worst is over, and then suddenly he throws in another unexpected element. I enjoy guessing what is coming based on context clues (e.g. in book one, when they were at Auntie Em's Garden Emporium and there were tons of horrified looking stone statues- If you know your Greek mythology, you know Medusa is coming!). 
 The only thing that drove me nuts about this book was how oblivious Percy seems to have become. In the first book, he's not well versed in mythology so Annabeth and Grover are often explaining what things are to him. If I suddenly discovered that all of those stories I'd learned in school were in fact real, I'd head home and hit the books to learn as much as I possibly could. I'd also become more aware of my surroundings. Percy, however, seems to have gone home and left his demigod self at Camp Half Blood for the year. He is fully aware of the "mist" and how it keeps humans from perceiving otherworldly things, but allows himself to be fooled by it on multiple occasions. He also requires a great deal of explanation from Annabeth regarding mythological stories. Percy has obviously never heard the quote, "Know thy enemy"! 
 This book is by no means a difficult read. It's obviously geared towards a younger crowd, but adults can definitely enjoy it as well! I'm 23, and I love what I've read thus far! I even went ahead and bought the remainder of the series! This book took me a grand total of two days to read, but part of that was because I couldn't put it down. It's well written, and you have the opportunity to learn more about the key characters and their lives, as well as gain more of the history of Camp Half Blood. 
 This second installment in the Percy Jackson series is exciting and interesting, taking the reader to many new places along the East coast of the United States. If you've got a child, or even if you enjoy a light read yourself, this book is the second installment in a series that has many great elements- adventure, mythology, action and more! Check it out!

Although harry potter was a children's book and put many 'grown up' novels to shame. Perhaps i'm the only one who sees the connection. Perhaps it is fabricated in my mind but this books sucks.

book_a.title: The Battle of the Labyrinth (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #4)

sample_reviews.review_text:
The Battle Of The Labyrinth (Percy Jackson And The Olympians #4), by Rick Riordan 
 Synopsis: Percy Jackson isn't expecting freshman orientation to be any fun. But when a mysterious mortal acquaintance appears on campus, followed by demon cheerleaders, things quickly move from bad to worse. 
 In this fourth installment of the blockbuster series, time is running out as war between the Olympians and the evil Titan lord Kronos draws near. Even the safe haven of Camp Half-Blood grows more vulnerable by the minute as Kronos's army prepares to invade its once impenetrable borders. To stop the invasion, Percy and his demigod friends must set out on a quest through the Labyrinth - a sprawling underground world with stunning surprises at every turn. 
 In A Sentence: A decent read, but I'm not feeling very wowed by this series (not yet anyway) 
 My Thoughts: At this point I admit I'm starting to just power through the series. It's a fun series that kids and young adults would really enjoy, but as an adult I don't feel as wowed as I could be. The chapter titles still pull a chuckle out of me, and there are sentences peppered throughout the story that are also pretty funny (case in point: "You hit the Lord of the Titans in the eye with a blue plastic hairbrush"). Ridiculous scenarios seem to be the main trademark of these books, which is always fun, but beyond that, the story doesn't hold a whole lot of depth. It's your typical action novels: lots of energy and a fast-paced plot, but very little depth and complexity. 
 Would I recommend this read? Of course! It's easy-going fun that doesn't require too much concentration. It's ridiculously funny in parts, and the incorporation of Greek Mythology into today's world is loads of fun to read about. Plus, it's a fast read, perfect for your next vacation. I'm starting the final book now and I'm looking forward to seeing how it ends. Happy reading!

 So many legends were woven into this book that I'm now feeling slightly dizzy - not that that's a bad thing. I like that the stories are growing more complicated. Also, having read books 2, 3 & 4 within a few days, I don't have clear delineations between them in my own mind - entirely my own fault! I think I'll take a short break before reading the final book - but not a very long one, because I'm looking forward to finding out how the overall story ends.

Goblet of Fire is the bestest of best Harry Potter novels. book_b.title: The Battle of the Labyrinth (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, #4)

sample_reviews.review_text:
The Battle Of The Labyrinth (Percy Jackson And The Olympians #4), by Rick Riordan 
 Synopsis: Percy Jackson isn't expecting freshman orientation to be any fun. But when a mysterious mortal acquaintance appears on campus, followed by demon cheerleaders, things quickly move from bad to worse. 
 In this fourth installment of the blockbuster series, time is running out as war between the Olympians and the evil Titan lord Kronos draws near. Even the safe haven of Camp Half-Blood grows more vulnerable by the minute as Kronos's army prepares to invade its once impenetrable borders. To stop the invasion, Percy and his demigod friends must set out on a quest through the Labyrinth - a sprawling underground world with stunning surprises at every turn. 
 In A Sentence: A decent read, but I'm not feeling very wowed by this series (not yet anyway) 
 My Thoughts: At this point I admit I'm starting to just power through the series. It's a fun series that kids and young adults would really enjoy, but as an adult I don't feel as wowed as I could be. The chapter titles still pull a chuckle out of me, and there are sentences peppered throughout the story that are also pretty funny (case in point: "You hit the Lord of the Titans in the eye with a blue plastic hairbrush"). Ridiculous scenarios seem to be the main trademark of these books, which is always fun, but beyond that, the story doesn't hold a whole lot of depth. It's your typical action novels: lots of energy and a fast-paced plot, but very little depth and complexity. 
 Would I recommend this read? Of course! It's easy-going fun that doesn't require too much concentration. It's ridiculously funny in parts, and the incorporation of Greek Mythology into today's world is loads of fun to read about. Plus, it's a fast read, perfect for your next vacation. I'm starting the final book now and I'm looking forward to seeing how it ends. Happy reading!

This series keeps getting better and better. When I was a kid I had always liked the stories of Icarus and Dadeulus. This series is enjoyable and engaging now, if I had read them as a kid I would have been obsessed with them.

I'm not sure what I said for the Titan's Curse by Rick Riordan, but honestly, this book is my fave so far. I can't even remember what happened in the Titan's Curse because I was just sooo intrigued by this storyline. A job well done!
This series actually groves on me. It is pretty good

Still really enjoying this series. I find it interesting that, as Percy and his friends grow up, the gods are shown less as the all-powerful 15 foot high beings of the earlier books, and instead as rather more 'human' figures. Big fat metaphor for teenagers learning to relate to the adults in their lives, perhaps? I know that even though neither made long appearances, I loved both Poseidon and Dionysus in this book. 
 So many legends were woven into this book that I'm now feeling slightly dizzy - not that that's a bad thing. I like that the stories are growing more complicated. Also, having read books 2, 3 & 4 within a few days, I don't have clear delineations between them in my own mind - entirely my own fault! I think I'll take a short break before reading the final book - but not a very long one, because I'm looking forward to finding out how the overall story ends. 
 Read for the Seasonal Reading Challenge Winter 09/10 task 10.4 (Winner's Choice: Kari )

The multiple dream sequences to advance the story. We both felt that this distracted from the story. Personally I believe dream sequences are a lazy crutch authors use when they can't think of a way to logically advance part of the story.

 Don't get me wrong, the Harry Potter series (the first four at least) can be enchanting, engaging and a truly worthy read... 
 ... BUT it's not worth the hype. I could name HUNDREDS of books and a score of series that would be a better use of your time than HP but, sadly, did not receive the "hype" this series did. But starting at the fifth book, the story begins to fall off track.

 Over all, I would tell you to try the series out. It's one of the few series out there that I believe will have some historical value because of that fact. 
 If you are looking for an astoundingly great read, however... 
 ... look elsewhere.(

Malfoy always taunts Harry, Ron, and Hermione. Snape always hates Harry and the Griffyndors for no apparent reason, and his bias is never questioned. Lee Jordan always swears at the Quidditch matches and gets scolded by McGonnogal. Harry always manages to barely catch the snitch just in time to win a Quidditch match for Gryffindor. Harry and Ron always suck at classes while Hermione gets shamed for doing well. 
 See how I revealed no spoilers there? 
 There's only so much of the same thing you can read over and over again before it all blends together into a boring mess. Five books of this?! With the plot drawn out for hundreds of useless pages? Why would I want to endure three ignorant teenagers complaining about not being told anything, while they whisper secrets in the open and lazily sit by watching the action go on around them? Why can't I be in on the big-kids' table, and help the adults put things together? While reading this I constantly had to ask myself... How are these good characters again? There's something wrong when the two-dimensional side characters are more intriguing than your three musketeers. 
 Hmm, I wonder why it's so hard to ignore the school bully long enough, so you can keep playing your favorite sport, Harry? 
 Hmm, it must be hard to control a conversation long enough to say what you want to your own godfather, Harry. 
 Hmm, so you want to "burn" the useful gift your brilliant friend gave you for help, Harry? You and your best friend pay no attention when Hermione, the successful student, tries to help your study schedule (never thought that might help you become an Auror, did you, Harry?). That must have something to do with the fact that you haven't yet realized how reading actually helps in real life, dear Harry. 
 Hmm, I wonder why it's a bad idea your mind is linked with Voldemort's, Harry. 
 Hmm, could it be a good idea to guard your mind from your worst enemy, Harry? 
 Hmm, how about you stop complaining and learn from the people you envy or criticize, Harry? 
 Please tell me why anyone would like reading 600 pages of dull plot surrounding this guy's attitude problems? I don't get it. 
 The only new material in this one is Umbridge's infernal presence, which was entertaining. But Rowling took 800+ pages to retell the same story she's done four times before, inserting maybe 20% new material, while boring me with the rest of the useless rambling junk. Stop killing so many trees and use less of my time. Stop asking so many questions, and make something actually happen. Stop writing about hormonal teenager problems, and give me morality and suspense. Give fewer homework troubles to your idiot main character, and describe more of the legacy behind everything actually driving this plot. Stop feeding me the same patronizing slop... I can see through it. 
 At least the last 200 pages are interesting. 
 Why are all the side characters seemingly more interesting than the protagonist? It's because Rowling refuses to actually use the entire 800 pages for character development. Instead she crams all the good action into the last 5-7 chapters (making me guilty for feeling happy, after struggling through the slothful 600 previous pages). 
 This book earns 3 stars only for Rowling's inventive creations in the wizarding world, and the last 7 chapters which made the whole 800+ pages of drudgery somewhat worth it. But when the environment is more interesting than the plot... Errrrr... There's a problem. 
 I'm sorry, but if you've failed to make your hero interesting by the fifth book, just stop... stop using your international fame to put me through this mediocre excuse for a saga... It was interesting in book one, Rowling, because that one was 200 pages. And maybe you could pass it by me again in book two. But no more... Please no eighth book... Please, I'm begging you... 
 *sigh* Now on to book six: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince. I'm gonna guess that the next 800+ pages have more of the same idiotic lines from Ron that pass for quality children's literature...

So much of the expert advice on writing is about advancing the plot, moving the story ahead, cutting out unnecessary detail. Harry Potter 5 breaks those rules, and it's a better book for it. 
 All this is old news, but I re-read most of The Order of The Phoenix over the holidays, just because I like it so much. And also because I appreciate its brief but gentle treatment of mental illness. 
 My absolute favorite scene is when Neville, a minor character, realizes his friends know that his parents are mentally ill. His bossy grandmother is there, and she tells him what to do and how to feel. But Neville takes his own approach, which is shyer, sweeter and in the end much more courageous. 
 Another wonderful minor character was the socially awkward Luna Lovegood. My favorite scene with her is at the very end of the book, when Harry stumbles onto Luna in the hall on the last day of the term. At first he wants to hide from her. Then, when he realizes that she knows how odd she seems to everyone else, he feels sorry for her. By the time he walks away, he is very glad to have talked to her. 
 I thought it was sad when Luna told Harry that their schoolmates played tricks on her. Bret disagreed. "She wasn't sad about it," he said. "She was handling it just fine." 
 And she was--which may explain why her strangeness is so likable. 
 She and the clumsy but determined Neville are the reasons I've read Harry Potter 5 more than once.

Harry Potter. Everyone has at least heard of the story. This is actually my third time reading the book, and I have to say after reading so many children's books, I can see what it has taken the world by storm. 
 Harry Potter is orphaned as a baby and send to live with his terrible uncle and aunt, the Dursleys. His cousin, Dudley, is the same age as Harry, and bullies him. Harry's bedroom is the tiny room under the stairs, meanwhile, Dudley has two bedrooms, one to sleep in and one for all of his toys! This is the life that Harry has lived for the past ten years. Then one day a letter arrives for him, but instead of being allowed to read it, his uncle keeps them from Harry. But there is no escape. A giant, named Hagrid shows up and explains to Harry what his aunt and uncle have been hiding; Harry is a wizard! 
 Next thing Harry knows he is off to a special school where he finally makes friends. He also has some enemies, but for the first time in his life, he feels like he belongs. I love the way this book is written. There is humor and creativity. Harry finds himself in one adventure after another, and he also learns what it is like to have people care for you. Great book that really will appeal to all ages, not just the target audience of a middle grade reader.

The book with the greatest potential and the greatest let down.

But starting at the fifth book, the story begins to fall off track. 
 The sixth book was downright disappointing, the fact that a FAN GIRL gets the hero annoyed me, the seventh book, had it's moments, I admit but Rowling should be shot for that pathetic epilogue. I've seen better writing from ten year olds and I am not exaggerating. 
 Over all, I would tell you to try the series out. It's been a great gate-way book into other (more worthy) fantasy books for many, many people and HAS convinced many kids out there that reading can be fun! It's one of the few series out there that I believe will have some historical value because of that fact. 
 If you are looking for an astoundingly great read, however...

Malfoy always taunts Harry, Ron, and Hermione. Snape always hates Harry and the Griffyndors for no apparent reason, and his bias is never questioned. Lee Jordan always swears at the Quidditch matches and gets scolded by McGonnogal. Harry always manages to barely catch the snitch just in time to win a Quidditch match for Gryffindor. Harry and Ron always suck at classes while Hermione gets shamed for doing well. 
 See how I revealed no spoilers there? 
 There's only so much of the same thing you can read over and over again before it all blends together into a boring mess. Five books of this?! With the plot drawn out for hundreds of useless pages? Why would I want to endure three ignorant teenagers complaining about not being told anything, while they whisper secrets in the open and lazily sit by watching the action go on around them? Why can't I be in on the big-kids' table, and help the adults put things together? While reading this I constantly had to ask myself... How are these good characters again? There's something wrong when the two-dimensional side characters are more intriguing than your three musketeers. 
 Hmm, I wonder why it's so hard to ignore the school bully long enough, so you can keep playing your favorite sport, Harry? 
 Hmm, it must be hard to control a conversation long enough to say what you want to your own godfather, Harry. 
 Hmm, so you want to "burn" the useful gift your brilliant friend gave you for help, Harry? You and your best friend pay no attention when Hermione, the successful student, tries to help your study schedule (never thought that might help you become an Auror, did you, Harry?). That must have something to do with the fact that you haven't yet realized how reading actually helps in real life, dear Harry. 
 Hmm, I wonder why it's a bad idea your mind is linked with Voldemort's, Harry. 
 Hmm, could it be a good idea to guard your mind from your worst enemy, Harry? 
 Hmm, how about you stop complaining and learn from the people you envy or criticize, Harry? 
 Please tell me why anyone would like reading 600 pages of dull plot surrounding this guy's attitude problems? I don't get it. 
 The only new material in this one is Umbridge's infernal presence, which was entertaining. But Rowling took 800+ pages to retell the same story she's done four times before, inserting maybe 20% new material, while boring me with the rest of the useless rambling junk. Stop killing so many trees and use less of my time. Stop asking so many questions, and make something actually happen. Stop writing about hormonal teenager problems, and give me morality and suspense. Give fewer homework troubles to your idiot main character, and describe more of the legacy behind everything actually driving this plot. Stop feeding me the same patronizing slop... I can see through it. 
 At least the last 200 pages are interesting. 
 Why are all the side characters seemingly more interesting than the protagonist? It's because Rowling refuses to actually use the entire 800 pages for character development. Instead she crams all the good action into the last 5-7 chapters (making me guilty for feeling happy, after struggling through the slothful 600 previous pages). 
 This book earns 3 stars only for Rowling's inventive creations in the wizarding world, and the last 7 chapters which made the whole 800+ pages of drudgery somewhat worth it. But when the environment is more interesting than the plot... Errrrr... There's a problem. 
 I'm sorry, but if you've failed to make your hero interesting by the fifth book, just stop... stop using your international fame to put me through this mediocre excuse for a saga... It was interesting in book one, Rowling, because that one was 200 pages. And maybe you could pass it by me again in book two. But no more... Please no eighth book... Please, I'm begging you... 
 *sigh* Now on to book six: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince. I'm gonna guess that the next 800+ pages have more of the same idiotic lines from Ron that pass for quality children's literature...

So much of the expert advice on writing is about advancing the plot, moving the story ahead, cutting out unnecessary detail. Harry Potter 5 breaks those rules, and it's a better book for it. 
 All this is old news, but I re-read most of The Order of The Phoenix over the holidays, just because I like it so much. And also because I appreciate its brief but gentle treatment of mental illness. 
 My absolute favorite scene is when Neville, a minor character, realizes his friends know that his parents are mentally ill. His bossy grandmother is there, and she tells him what to do and how to feel. But Neville takes his own approach, which is shyer, sweeter and in the end much more courageous. 
 Another wonderful minor character was the socially awkward Luna Lovegood. My favorite scene with her is at the very end of the book, when Harry stumbles onto Luna in the hall on the last day of the term. At first he wants to hide from her. Then, when he realizes that she knows how odd she seems to everyone else, he feels sorry for her. By the time he walks away, he is very glad to have talked to her. 
 I thought it was sad when Luna told Harry that their schoolmates played tricks on her. Bret disagreed. "She wasn't sad about it," he said. "She was handling it just fine." 
 And she was--which may explain why her strangeness is so likable. 
 She and the clumsy but determined Neville are the reasons I've read Harry Potter 5 more than once.

Harry Potter. Everyone has at least heard of the story. This is actually my third time reading the book, and I have to say after reading so many children's books, I can see what it has taken the world by storm. 
 Harry Potter is orphaned as a baby and send to live with his terrible uncle and aunt, the Dursleys. His cousin, Dudley, is the same age as Harry, and bullies him. Harry's bedroom is the tiny room under the stairs, meanwhile, Dudley has two bedrooms, one to sleep in and one for all of his toys! This is the life that Harry has lived for the past ten years. Then one day a letter arrives for him, but instead of being allowed to read it, his uncle keeps them from Harry. But there is no escape. A giant, named Hagrid shows up and explains to Harry what his aunt and uncle have been hiding; Harry is a wizard! 
 Next thing Harry knows he is off to a special school where he finally makes friends. He also has some enemies, but for the first time in his life, he feels like he belongs. I love the way this book is written. There is humor and creativity. Harry finds himself in one adventure after another, and he also learns what it is like to have people care for you. Great book that really will appeal to all ages, not just the target audience of a middle grade reader.
